docs.title: Inro
docs.text: Inro is a PyTorch package for implicit neural representations (INRs): a unified framework for implementing, training and evaluating them. It features the official implementation of FUTON, introduced in our paper, and major INR architectures such as SIREN, FINER, RFF, Instant-NGP and TensoRF behind one interface. Reusable components and pipelines cover image and volume representation and novel view synthesis.

docs.title: FUTON against the strongest baseline
docs.text:
Every model of a task has the same parameter budget, and times are median training times per signal on an A100, from the same runs as the scores. FUTON makes the best trade-off of speed and reconstruction quality on every task.

Images, Kodak

+0.90 dB

37.63 dB against MFN's 36.72, in 4.1 s against 57.3 s.

Occupancy, Stanford

+0.21 %

99.90 % IoU against GA-Planes' 99.69 %, in 5.4 s against 62.2 s.

Radiance fields, Blender

+0.60 dB

29.22 dB against FINER's 28.62, in 152 s against 219 s.

docs.title: How FUTON works
docs.text:
Most INRs hide their prior in the nonlinearity: sines, Gabor wavelets, Gaussians, or a hash-grid lookup in front of a ReLU network. FUTON puts the prior in the parameterization: the signal is expanded in a fixed basis along each coordinate axis, and the coefficient tensor of that expansion is stored in low-rank form.

  • Fast

    A point costs \(O(CKR)\) for \(C\) axes, \(K\) basis functions per axis and rank \(R\). On a grid, each axis is evaluated once per distinct coordinate and shared by every point on it.

  • Accurate at equal size

    At matched parameter counts FUTON leads every baseline on the average of Kodak images, Stanford occupancy volumes and Blender radiance fields.

  • Transparent

    With a linear head FUTON is a rank-\(R\) CP model of the signal in the chosen basis, so bandwidth (\(K\)) and capacity (\(R\)) are explicit knobs, with a computable error bound.

docs.title: See the difference
docs.text: SIREN, 33.72 dB FUTON, 37.93 dB Drag across a crop of kodim19. Both models hold about 197k parameters, and each score is over the whole image. The lego scene in orbit, at about 75k parameters per model, with the test-view PSNR.

docs.title: One interface
docs.text:
Every model maps coordinates in \([-1, 1]\) to values, so one training call fits them all.

import torch
import inro

dataset = inro.ImageCoordinateDataset("data/Kodak/kodim19.png")  # (1)!
H, W, _ = dataset.target.shape

model = inro.FUTON(  # (2)!
    in_features=2,
    out_features=3,
    basis=("cosine", {"num_components": [H // 2, W // 2]}),
    combiner=("cp", {"rank": 280}),
    head=("mlp", {"hidden_layers": 1, "hidden_features": 64}),  # (3)!
    output_activation=torch.tanh,
)

result = inro.train(model, dataset, dataset, num_steps=1000, lr=1e-1, metrics={"psnr": inro.psnr})
print(result["history"][-1]["eval"])  # {"psnr": 37.8}
  1. Any RGB image: a path, a tensor or a PIL image. Each access returns every pixel's coordinates and color.
  2. Swap in any other model of the zoo, such as inro.SIREN(2, 3, hidden_features=256, hidden_layers=4, output_activation=torch.tanh). The training call stays the same.
  3. An MLP with one hidden layer 64 wide, whose first layer reads a whole image off the combiner's grid in one contraction.

docs.title: Citation
docs.text:
If you use Inro or FUTON in your research, please cite the paper:

@article{ashtari2026futon,
  title   = {{FUTON}: Fourier Tensor Network for Implicit Neural Representations},
  author  = {Ashtari, Pooya and Behmandpoor, Pourya and Deligiannis, Nikos and Pi{\v{z}}urica, Aleksandra},
  journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2602.13414},
  year    = {2026}

The name comes from the inrō, a Japanese case of stacked compartments. The logo is a disc of three compartments, cut by two cosines of rising frequency, as in FUTON's Fourier basis. The code is released under the MIT license.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: The problems that come up first, and what to do about them.

docs.title: Coordinates and targets
docs.text:
The fit is poor or the loss does not move

Coordinates must lie in \([-1, 1]\) on every axis. The coordinate datasets generate them that way, and FUTON's bases and the hash and feature grids are all defined on that domain. Do not pre-normalize to \([0, 1]\). Targets from the datasets are in \([-1, 1]\) too (occupancy in \(\{-1, 1\}\)), which is why the benchmark models end in output_activation=torch.tanh and why the default loss reports PSNR for that range.

ValueError: radius must be >= 1 and num_components >= 2 * radius

A local basis (triangle, lanczos) needs at least 2 * radius components per axis: 2 for the triangle, 6 for Lanczos-3. With num_components=[H // 2, W // 2] this is never an issue for real images; it is for tiny test inputs.

grid_size on a dataset and subsample together

ImageCoordinateDataset(image, grid_size=...) evaluates a model on another grid than the image's, for example a finer one, and cannot subsample; it is for evaluation.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
CUDA out of memory during evaluation

Pass chunk_size to inro.train, inro.evaluate or inro.chunked_inference; the occupancy benchmark evaluates volumes of 17 to 62 million voxels with chunk_size=2**20. In inro.nerf.train, lower num_rays or max_samples_per_ray; in inro.nerf.evaluate and render_image, pass chunk_size (rays per pass).

CUDA out of memory during training

Draw fewer coordinates per step with subsample (a fraction) or max_samples (a count); the benchmarks train on the whole image and on 1,048,576 voxels per step.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
NerfAcc: No CUDA toolkit found. NerfAcc will be disabled.

nerfacc builds its CUDA extension on first use and needs nvcc for that. Without it, inro.nerf.create_renderer() selects the PyTorch renderer, which produces the same renders more slowly; training still works. Install a CUDA toolkit matching your PyTorch build to use nerfacc.

docs.title: Data and extras
docs.text:
ModuleNotFoundError: trimesh (or mcubes, open3d)

Meshes as occupancy volumes, mesh export and offscreen rendering need the 3d extra: pip install -e ".[3d]". Point clouds in .xyz format load without it.

No .png from OccupancyCoordinateDataset.save

It renders offscreen with Open3D, which needs EGL and a GPU driver but no display. Where the renderer cannot start, save warns and writes the mesh alone.

LPIPS downloads weights on first use

inro.lpips loads the VGG (or AlexNet) backbone through torchmetrics, which fetches the weights once. On a machine without internet access, run one evaluation on a connected one first, with the same cache directory.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
A run is skipped with \"holds a run of a different setup\"

Runs are keyed by model name inside the log directory. After changing a model's entry in a config, pass --overwrite to rerun it in place, or give the variant its own name or --log-dir.

A model diverges

Learning rates in the configs come from the grid {3e-1, 1e-1, 3e-2, 1e-2, 3e-3, 1e-3, 3e-4, 1e-4}, each the best of the grid on two signals of the task, as each config's header says. Sine networks (SIREN, FINER) are the most sensitive; FUTON trains at 1e-2 to 1e-1 across tasks.

Training times differ from the tables

Times vary with the machine and its load; the tables take every cost from the benchmark runs themselves, each the median over a task's signals, as the reproduction page explains.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
What does hidden_layers count?

Hidden layers. A network with hidden_layers=h has h + 1 weight layers (MFN: h Gabor filters and h linear layers). The configs state the counts as the constructors expect them.

Loading an MLP checkpoint

MLP.layers contains only weight layers, so a network with hidden_layers=h has keys layers.0 to layers.h; a shared activation with parameters (for example nn.PReLU) lives under activation.*.

Reading the docstrings

docs.title: Compression
docs.text:
An INR is a compressed representation of its signal: the parameters are the code. inro.compression makes this concrete for FUTON, with a codec that fits a quantized model and serializes it, PIL codecs as baselines, and one function that measures any codec's rate-distortion point.

  1. Fita FUTON, under a rate-distortion loss
  2. Quantizeevery parameter tensor
  3. Packcodes and model settings, gzipped
  4. Rebuildthe model from the bytes
  5. Evaluateit on the pixel grid

docs.title: A codec in two calls
docs.text:
from torchvision.io import ImageReadMode, read_image
import inro

image = read_image("data/Kodak/kodim19.png", mode=ImageReadMode.RGB)  # uint8 (3, H, W)

encoded = inro.compression.encode_futon(
    image,
    basis=("cosine", {"num_components": 128}),
    combiner=("cp", {"rank": 64}),
    head="linear",
    num_steps=500,
    lr=0.1,
    alpha=0.005,
    quant_max=127,
)
reconstruction = inro.compression.decode_futon(encoded)  # uint8 (3, H, W)

encode_futon builds a FUTON from the keyword arguments (in_features and out_features default to 2 and the channel count), trains it with inro.rate_distortion_loss, quantizes every parameter tensor to quant_max levels, and packs the integer codes, their scales, the model configuration, the image ID and the spatial shape into gzip-compressed bytes. decode_futon rebuilds the model from those bytes and evaluates it on the pixel grid. The specs must be registry keys or (key, dict) pairs so that they survive the round trip. The linear head reads a whole image off the grid in one contraction.

The rate-distortion loss is \(\text{MSE} + \alpha \cdot H\), where \(H\) is the size-weighted mean of a Laplace entropy estimate of each parameter tensor, in bits; alpha=0 disables the rate term. quant_interval rounds the parameters to the quantization grid every so many steps during training, so that the model adapts to it (quantization-aware training); the final quantization always runs.

docs.title: Measuring a codec
docs.text:
futon = inro.compression.evaluate_compression(
    image,
    inro.compression.encode_futon,
    inro.compression.decode_futon,
    basis=("cosine", {"num_components": 128}),
    combiner=("cp", {"rank": 64}),
    head="linear",
    num_steps=500,
)
jpeg = inro.compression.evaluate_compression(
    image, inro.compression.encode_pil, inro.compression.decode_pil, format="JPEG", quality=50
)
webp = inro.compression.evaluate_compression(
    image, inro.compression.encode_pil, inro.compression.decode_pil, format="WEBP", quality=50
)

Each call returns {"PSNR (dB)", "bit rate (bpp)", "encoding time (ms)", "decoding time (ms)"}, with the decoded image under "reconstructed" if return_reconstruction=True. PSNR uses data_range=255 and is infinite for a lossless codec.

The keyword arguments go to the encoder, so a rate-distortion curve is a loop over rank (or num_components, quant_max, alpha) for FUTON and over quality for the PIL codecs, and inro.LinePlot draws the curves:

records = [
    {"codec": "FUTON", "rank": rank, **inro.compression.evaluate_compression(
        image, inro.compression.encode_futon, inro.compression.decode_futon,
        basis=("cosine", {"num_components": 128}), combiner=("cp", {"rank": rank}), head="linear",
    )}
    for rank in (16, 32, 64, 128)
]
plot = inro.LinePlot(records)
fig, ax = plot.plot(x="bit rate (bpp)", y="PSNR (dB)", hue="codec")

encode_pil accepts a path, a file object, or a (channels, H, W) tensor and forwards its keyword arguments to PIL.Image.save; format is required because the image is written to memory.

docs.title: Quantization in the training loop
docs.text:
The same machinery is available in inro.train:

result = inro.train(
    model,
    train_set,
    eval_set,
    quantize=True,
    quant_max=127,
    quant_interval=100,
    metrics={"psnr": inro.psnr},
    rate_metrics={"bpp": inro.bits_per_pixel},
)

Every evaluation then scores a quantized copy of the model, and the rate metrics see its parameters serialized with inro.encode_dict (torch.save plus gzip). result["model_dict"] holds the integer codes and scales, which inro.uniform_dequantize(model, model_dict) loads back, and checkpoint.pt keeps the quantized weights as an ordinary state dict. inro.uniform_quantize(model, quant_max) and inro.uniform_dequantize are also usable on their own.

docs.title: Entropy coding
docs.text: Function Purpose inro.compression.encode_arithmetic(symbols, pmfs), decode_arithmetic Integer arithmetic coding with a separate probability mass function per position, for codecs that model the parameter distribution explicitly inro.soft_entropy A differentiable entropy estimate from soft histogram assignments inro.laplace_entropy The closed-form estimate that rate_distortion_loss uses

docs.title: codecs
docs.text:
Image codecs: PIL formats (JPEG, WebP, PNG, ...) and FUTON.

An encoder maps an image to bytes and a decoder maps the bytes back to an image tensor (channels, H, W), so evaluate_compression can benchmark any pair.

docs.title: encode_pil
docs.text:
encode_pil(image: str | PathLike[str] | IO[bytes] | Tensor, **kwargs: Any) -> bytes

Encode an image with a PIL codec.

Parameters:

  • image (str | PathLike[str] | IO[bytes] | Tensor) –

    Path or binary file object of an image that PIL can open, or an image tensor (channels, H, W), uint8 or floating-point in [0, 1].

  • **kwargs (Any, default: {} ) –

    Arguments of PIL.Image.Image.save. Must include format, such as "JPEG", "WEBP" or "PNG", because PIL cannot infer it for an in-memory buffer, and may include codec options such as quality.

Returns:

  • bytes –

    The encoded image file.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    If image is not a path, a binary file object or a tensor.

Examples:

>>> image = torch.randint(0, 256, (3, 32, 32), dtype=torch.uint8)
>>> encoded = encode_pil(image, format="JPEG", quality=50)
>>> decode_pil(encoded).shape
torch.Size([3, 32, 32])
Source code in inro/compression/codecs.py 
def encode_pil(
    image: str | os.PathLike[str] | IO[bytes] | Tensor, **kwargs: Any
) -> bytes:
    """Encode an image with a PIL codec.

    Args:
        image: Path or binary file object of an image that PIL can open, or an image
            tensor ``(channels, H, W)``, ``uint8`` or floating-point in ``[0, 1]``.
        **kwargs: Arguments of :meth:`PIL.Image.Image.save`. Must include ``format``,
            such as ``"JPEG"``, ``"WEBP"`` or ``"PNG"``, because PIL cannot infer it for
            an in-memory buffer, and may include codec options such as ``quality``.

    Returns:
        The encoded image file.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``image`` is not a path, a binary file object or a tensor.

    Examples:
        >>> image = torch.randint(0, 256, (3, 32, 32), dtype=torch.uint8)
        >>> encoded = encode_pil(image, format="JPEG", quality=50)
        >>> decode_pil(encoded).shape
        torch.Size([3, 32, 32])
    """
    if isinstance(image, (str, os.PathLike, io.IOBase)):
        pil_image = Image.open(image)
    elif isinstance(image, Tensor):
        pil_image = FT.to_pil_image(image)
    else:
        raise ValueError("image must be a string, Path, IO[bytes] or Tensor")

    buffer = io.BytesIO()
    pil_image.save(buffer, **kwargs)
    return buffer.getvalue()

def decode_pil(encoded: bytes) -> Tensor:
    """Decode an image file held in memory, such as the output of :func:`encode_pil`.

    Args:
        encoded: Bytes of an image file in any format PIL can read.

    Returns:
        Image ``(channels, H, W)``, with the channels of the stored PIL mode and
            ``uint8`` values for 8-bit images.
    """
    return FT.pil_to_tensor(Image.open(io.BytesIO(encoded)))

docs.title: encode_futon
docs.text:
encode_futon(image: str | PathLike[str] | Image | Tensor, *, subsample: float = 1.0, lr: float = 0.1, num_steps: int = 500, alpha: float = 0.005, quant_max: int = 127, quant_interval: int = -1, log_interval: int = 100, device: str | device | None = None, seed: int = 0, **kwargs: Any) -> bytes

Encode an image by fitting a FUTON and serializing its quantized parameters.

Training minimizes rate_distortion_loss.

Parameters:

  • image (str | PathLike[str] | Image | Tensor) –

    Path or PIL image, converted to RGB, or uint8 tensor (channels, H, W).

  • subsample (float, default: 1.0 ) –

    Fraction of pixels sampled at each step, in (0, 1].

  • lr (float, default: 0.1 ) –

    Initial learning rate of Adam.

  • num_steps (int, default: 500 ) –

    Number of training steps.

  • alpha (float, default: 0.005 ) –

    Weight of the parameters' Laplace entropy estimate in the loss.

  • quant_max (int, default: 127 ) –

    Largest integer level. Each parameter tensor is scaled by quant_max / max(abs(w)) and rounded.

  • quant_interval (int, default: -1 ) –

    Steps between fake quantizations of the model; non-positive values disable them. The final quantization always runs.

  • log_interval (int, default: 100 ) –

    Steps between history records; see train.

  • device (str | device | None, default: None ) –

    Device to run on; None uses CUDA when available, else the CPU.

  • seed (int, default: 0 ) –

    Seed of the global PyTorch RNG, set after the model is built, so it does not control its initialization.

  • **kwargs (Any, default: {} ) –

    Arguments of FUTON. basis, combiner and head are required, each a registry key or a (key, dict) pair, and every value must load with torch.load(weights_only=True). in_features and out_features default to 2 and the channel count.

Returns:

  • bytes –

    The integer codes, their scales, the model config, the image ID and the spatial shape, serialized with torch.save and gzip.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    If basis, combiner or head is missing, or is neither a registry key nor a (key, dict) pair.

Examples:

>>> image = torch.randint(0, 256, (3, 16, 16), dtype=torch.uint8)
>>> encoded = encode_futon(
...     image,
...     num_steps=2,
...     basis=("cosine", {"num_components": 8}),
...     combiner=("cp", {"rank": 8}),
...     head="linear",
... )
>>> decode_futon(encoded).shape
torch.Size([3, 16, 16])
Source code in inro/compression/codecs.py 
def encode_futon(
    image: str | os.PathLike[str] | Image.Image | Tensor,
    *,
    subsample: float = 1.0,
    lr: float = 0.1,
    num_steps: int = 500,
    alpha: float = 0.005,
    quant_max: int = 127,
    quant_interval: int = -1,
    log_interval: int = 100,
    device: str | torch.device | None = None,
    seed: int = 0,
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> bytes:
    """Encode an image by fitting a FUTON and serializing its quantized parameters.

    Training minimizes :func:`~inro.losses.rate_distortion_loss`.

    Args:
        image: Path or PIL image, converted to RGB, or ``uint8`` tensor
            ``(channels, H, W)``.
        subsample: Fraction of pixels sampled at each step, in ``(0, 1]``.
        lr: Initial learning rate of Adam.
        num_steps: Number of training steps.
        alpha: Weight of the parameters' Laplace entropy estimate in the loss.
        quant_max: Largest integer level. Each parameter tensor is scaled by
            ``quant_max / max(abs(w))`` and rounded.
        quant_interval: Steps between fake quantizations of the model; non-positive
            values disable them. The final quantization always runs.
        log_interval: Steps between history records; see :func:`train`.
        device: Device to run on; ``None`` uses CUDA when available, else the CPU.
        seed: Seed of the global PyTorch RNG, set after the model is built, so it does
            not control its initialization.
        **kwargs: Arguments of :class:`FUTON`. ``basis``, ``combiner`` and ``head``
            are required, each a registry key or a ``(key, dict)`` pair, and every value
            must load with ``torch.load(weights_only=True)``. ``in_features`` and
            ``out_features`` default to 2 and the channel count.

    Returns:
        The integer codes, their scales, the model config, the image ID and the spatial
            shape, serialized with ``torch.save`` and gzip.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``basis``, ``combiner`` or ``head`` is missing, or is neither
            a registry key nor a ``(key, dict)`` pair.

    Examples:
        >>> image = torch.randint(0, 256, (3, 16, 16), dtype=torch.uint8)
        >>> encoded = encode_futon(
        ...     image,
        ...     num_steps=2,
        ...     basis=("cosine", {"num_components": 8}),
        ...     combiner=("cp", {"rank": 8}),
        ...     head="linear",
        ... )
        >>> decode_futon(encoded).shape
        torch.Size([3, 16, 16])
    """
    for name in ("basis", "combiner", "head"):
        if name not in kwargs:
            raise ValueError(f"encode_futon requires the FUTON argument `{name}`")
        _check_module_spec(name, kwargs[name])

    dataset = ImageCoordinateDataset(image=image, subsample=subsample)
    model_config = {
        "in_features": dataset.input.shape[-1],
        "out_features": dataset.target.shape[-1],
        **kwargs,
    }
    model = FUTON(**model_config)
    train_results = train(
        model,
        dataset,
        loss_fn=partial(rate_distortion_loss, alpha=alpha),
        lr=lr,
        num_steps=num_steps,
        quantize=True,
        quant_max=quant_max,
        quant_interval=quant_interval,
        log_interval=log_interval,
        eval_interval=-1,
        device=device,
        seed=seed,
    )

    metadata = {
        "image": {"id": dataset.id, "shape": tuple(dataset.grid_size)},
        "model": {"config": model_config, "state": train_results["model_dict"]},
    }
    return encode_dict(metadata)

docs.text:
decode_futon(encoded: bytes, *, device: str | device | None = None) -> Tensor

Reconstruct an image from the bytes of encode_futon.

Rebuilds the stored FUTON, dequantizes its parameters and evaluates the whole coordinate grid in one pass. The output is clamped to [-1, 1] and mapped to uint8.

Parameters:

  • encoded (bytes) –

    Bytes returned by encode_futon.

  • device (str | device | None, default: None ) –

    Device to run on; None uses the default device.

Returns:

  • Tensor –

    Reconstructed uint8 image (channels, H, W) on device.

Source code in inro/compression/codecs.py 
def decode_futon(encoded: bytes, *, device: str | torch.device | None = None) -> Tensor:
    """Reconstruct an image from the bytes of :func:`encode_futon`.

    Rebuilds the stored FUTON, dequantizes its parameters and evaluates the whole
    coordinate grid in one pass. The output is clamped to ``[-1, 1]`` and mapped to
    ``uint8``.

    Args:
        encoded: Bytes returned by :func:`encode_futon`.
        device: Device to run on; ``None`` uses the default device.

    Returns:
        Reconstructed ``uint8`` image ``(channels, H, W)`` on ``device``.
    """
    metadata = decode_dict(encoded)
    model_config = metadata["model"]["config"]
    model_dict = metadata["model"]["state"]
    image_shape = metadata["image"]["shape"]

    coordinates = create_coordinates(image_shape).to(device)

    model = FUTON(**model_config)
    uniform_dequantize(model, model_dict)

    model.to(device)
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        output = model(coordinates)

    return ImageCoordinateDataset.postprocess(output)

evaluate_compression(image: Tensor, encode_fn: Callable[..., bytes], decode_fn: Callable[[bytes], Tensor], /, *, return_reconstruction: bool = False, **kwargs: Any) -> dict[str, float | Tensor]

Measure an image codec's PSNR, bit rate, and encoding and decoding times.

PSNR uses data_range=255 and is infinite for lossless codecs. Timings are wall-clock, from perf_counter, without CUDA synchronization.

Parameters:

  • image (Tensor) –

    Original uint8 image (channels, H, W).

  • encode_fn (Callable[..., bytes]) –

    Encoder, called as encode_fn(image, **kwargs).

  • decode_fn (Callable[[bytes], Tensor]) –

    Decoder, called as decode_fn(encoded); its result must be on the device of image.

  • return_reconstruction (bool, default: False ) –

    Whether to include the decoded image in the result.

  • **kwargs (Any, default: {} ) –

    Arguments of the encoder.

Returns:

  • dict[str, float | Tensor] –

    Dictionary with the floats "PSNR (dB)", "bit rate (bpp)", "encoding time (ms)" and "decoding time (ms)", and, if requested, the decoded tensor "reconstructed".

Examples:

>>> import torch
>>> from inro.compression import decode_pil, encode_pil
>>> image = torch.randint(0, 256, (3, 32, 32), dtype=torch.uint8)
>>> results = evaluate_compression(image, encode_pil, decode_pil, format="PNG")
>>> results["PSNR (dB)"]
inf
Source code in inro/compression/evaluation.py 
def evaluate_compression(
    image: Tensor,
    encode_fn: Callable[..., bytes],
    decode_fn: Callable[[bytes], Tensor],
    /,
    *,
    return_reconstruction: bool = False,
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> dict[str, float | Tensor]:
    """Measure an image codec's PSNR, bit rate, and encoding and decoding times.

    PSNR uses ``data_range=255`` and is infinite for lossless codecs. Timings are
    wall-clock, from ``perf_counter``, without CUDA synchronization.

    Args:
        image: Original ``uint8`` image ``(channels, H, W)``.
        encode_fn: Encoder, called as ``encode_fn(image, **kwargs)``.
        decode_fn: Decoder, called as ``decode_fn(encoded)``; its result must be on the
            device of ``image``.
        return_reconstruction: Whether to include the decoded image in the result.
        **kwargs: Arguments of the encoder.

    Returns:
        Dictionary with the floats ``"PSNR (dB)"``, ``"bit rate (bpp)"``,
            ``"encoding time (ms)"`` and ``"decoding time (ms)"``, and, if requested,
            the decoded tensor ``"reconstructed"``.

    Examples:
        >>> import torch
        >>> from inro.compression import decode_pil, encode_pil
        >>> image = torch.randint(0, 256, (3, 32, 32), dtype=torch.uint8)
        >>> results = evaluate_compression(image, encode_pil, decode_pil, format="PNG")
        >>> results["PSNR (dB)"]
        inf
    """
    start_time = time.perf_counter()
    encoded = encode_fn(image, **kwargs)
    encoding_time = 1000 * (time.perf_counter() - start_time)

    start_time = time.perf_counter()
    reconstruction = decode_fn(encoded)
    decoding_time = 1000 * (time.perf_counter() - start_time)

    results: dict[str, float | Tensor] = {
        "PSNR (dB)": psnr(reconstruction, image),
        "bit rate (bpp)": bits_per_pixel(encoded, image),
        "encoding time (ms)": encoding_time,
        "decoding time (ms)": decoding_time,
    }

    if return_reconstruction:
        results["reconstructed"] = reconstruction

    return results

docs.title: arithmetic_coding
docs.text:
Integer arithmetic coding with per-position probability mass functions.

Every position of a symbol sequence is coded under its own probability mass function (PMF), and alphabet sizes may differ between positions. PMFs are scaled to integer frequency tables and coded with a 32-bit integer arithmetic coder using bit-plus-follow (underflow) renormalization.

References

Witten et al., "Arithmetic Coding for Data Compression", Communications of the ACM 1987.

docs.title: encode_arithmetic
docs.text:
encode_arithmetic(symbols: Tensor | ndarray | Sequence[int], pmfs: list[_PMF] | tuple[_PMF, ...], precision: int = 1 << 16) -> bytes

Encode a symbol sequence with arithmetic coding.

Position i is coded under its own PMF pmfs[i], and alphabet sizes may differ between positions. Every symbol must have nonzero probability under its PMF: a zero-probability symbol is not rejected and silently corrupts the bitstream.

Parameters:

  • symbols (Tensor | ndarray | Sequence[int]) –

    Integer symbols, flattened to (N,). A tensor must be on the CPU.

  • pmfs (list[_PMF] | tuple[_PMF, ...]) –

    List or tuple of N PMFs, where pmfs[i][k] is the probability of symbol k at position i, not necessarily normalized. Each PMF is a tensor on any device, a NumPy array or a sequence of floats.

  • precision (int, default: 1 << 16 ) –

    Total integer frequency each PMF is scaled to, a count rather than a number of bits. Nonzero probabilities keep a frequency of at least 1, so the total can slightly exceed it. Must match decode_arithmetic.

Returns:

  • bytes –

    A 4-byte big-endian uint32 symbol count N followed by the bitstream.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    If pmfs is not a list or tuple of length N, a PMF is empty, has a negative entry or sums to zero, or a symbol is outside the alphabet of its PMF.

Examples:

>>> pmfs = [[0.7, 0.3], [0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.4, 0.6]]
>>> encoded = encode_arithmetic([0, 2, 1], pmfs)
>>> decode_arithmetic(encoded, pmfs)
array([0, 2, 1])
Source code in inro/compression/arithmetic_coding.py 
def encode_arithmetic(
    symbols: Tensor | np.ndarray | Sequence[int],
    pmfs: list[_PMF] | tuple[_PMF, ...],
    precision: int = 1 << 16,
) -> bytes:
    """Encode a symbol sequence with arithmetic coding.

    Position ``i`` is coded under its own PMF ``pmfs[i]``, and alphabet sizes may differ
    between positions. Every symbol must have nonzero probability under its PMF: a
    zero-probability symbol is not rejected and silently corrupts the bitstream.

    Args:
        symbols: Integer symbols, flattened to ``(N,)``. A tensor must be on the CPU.
        pmfs: List or tuple of ``N`` PMFs, where ``pmfs[i][k]`` is the probability of
            symbol ``k`` at position ``i``, not necessarily normalized. Each PMF is a
            tensor on any device, a NumPy array or a sequence of floats.
        precision: Total integer frequency each PMF is scaled to, a count rather than a
            number of bits. Nonzero probabilities keep a frequency of at least ``1``, so
            the total can slightly exceed it. Must match :func:`decode_arithmetic`.

    Returns:
        A 4-byte big-endian ``uint32`` symbol count ``N`` followed by the bitstream.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``pmfs`` is not a list or tuple of length ``N``, a PMF is empty,
            has a negative entry or sums to zero, or a symbol is outside the alphabet of
            its PMF.

    Examples:
        >>> pmfs = [[0.7, 0.3], [0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.4, 0.6]]
        >>> encoded = encode_arithmetic([0, 2, 1], pmfs)
        >>> decode_arithmetic(encoded, pmfs)
        array([0, 2, 1])
    """
    symbols = np.asarray(symbols, dtype=np.int64).ravel()
    num_symbols = symbols.size
    if not isinstance(pmfs, (list, tuple)) or len(pmfs) != num_symbols:
        raise ValueError("pmfs must be a list/tuple with same length as symbols")
    tables = _frequency_tables(pmfs, precision)

    writer = _BitWriter()
    low = 0
    high = _MAX_STATE
    pending_bits = 0

    def write_bit_with_pending(bit: int) -> None:
        nonlocal pending_bits
        writer.write_bit(bit)
        while pending_bits > 0:
            writer.write_bit(1 - bit)
            pending_bits -= 1

    for index, symbol in enumerate(symbols):
        cumulative, total = tables[index]
        alphabet_size = len(cumulative) - 1
        if symbol < 0 or symbol >= alphabet_size:
            raise ValueError(
                f"symbol {symbol} out of range for PMF at position {index}"
            )
        interval_size = high - low + 1
        high = low + (interval_size * int(cumulative[symbol + 1]) // total) - 1
        low = low + (interval_size * int(cumulative[symbol]) // total)

        # Emit a shared leading bit; defer bits while the interval straddles 1/2.
        while True:
            if high < _HALF:
                write_bit_with_pending(0)
            elif low >= _HALF:
                write_bit_with_pending(1)
                low -= _HALF
                high -= _HALF
            elif low >= _QUARTER and high < _THREE_QUARTERS:
                pending_bits += 1
                low -= _QUARTER
                high -= _QUARTER
            else:
                break
            low = (low << 1) & _MAX_STATE
            high = ((high << 1) & _MAX_STATE) | 1

    # One final bit and the deferred bits identify the remaining interval.
    pending_bits += 1
    write_bit_with_pending(0 if low < _QUARTER else 1)

    return struct.pack(">I", num_symbols) + writer.finish()

docs.title: decode_arithmetic
docs.text:
decode_arithmetic(encoded: bytes, pmfs: list[_PMF] | tuple[_PMF, ...], precision: int = 1 << 16) -> ndarray

Decode a bitstream produced by encode_arithmetic.

Parameters:

  • encoded (bytes) –

    Bytes returned by encode_arithmetic.

  • pmfs (list[_PMF] | tuple[_PMF, ...]) –

    List or tuple of the PMFs used for encoding, one per symbol.

  • precision (int, default: 1 << 16 ) –

    The precision used for encoding.

Returns:

  • ndarray –

    The decoded symbols, an int64 array (N,).

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    If encoded is shorter than the 4-byte header, pmfs is not a list or tuple whose length equals the encoded symbol count, or a PMF is empty, has a negative entry or sums to zero.

Source code in inro/compression/arithmetic_coding.py 
def decode_arithmetic(
    encoded: bytes,
    pmfs: list[_PMF] | tuple[_PMF, ...],
    precision: int = 1 << 16,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Decode a bitstream produced by :func:`encode_arithmetic`.

    Args:
        encoded: Bytes returned by :func:`encode_arithmetic`.
        pmfs: List or tuple of the PMFs used for encoding, one per symbol.
        precision: The ``precision`` used for encoding.

    Returns:
        The decoded symbols, an ``int64`` array ``(N,)``.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``encoded`` is shorter than the 4-byte header, ``pmfs`` is not a
            list or tuple whose length equals the encoded symbol count, or a PMF is
            empty, has a negative entry or sums to zero.
    """
    if len(encoded) < 4:
        raise ValueError("Input too short")
    num_symbols = struct.unpack(">I", encoded[:4])[0]
    if not isinstance(pmfs, (list, tuple)) or len(pmfs) != num_symbols:
        raise ValueError(
            "pmfs must be a list/tuple with same length as encoded symbols"
        )
    tables = _frequency_tables(pmfs, precision)

    reader = _BitReader(encoded[4:])
    value = 0
    for _ in range(_STATE_BITS):
        value = (value << 1) | reader.read_bit()

    low = 0
    high = _MAX_STATE
    symbols = np.zeros(num_symbols, dtype=np.int64)

    for index, (cumulative, total) in enumerate(tables):
        interval_size = high - low + 1
        scaled = ((value - low + 1) * total - 1) // interval_size
        # Find the symbol whose cumulative-frequency interval contains scaled.
        symbol = max(bisect_right(cumulative, int(scaled)) - 1, 0)
        symbols[index] = symbol

        high = low + (interval_size * int(cumulative[symbol + 1]) // total) - 1
        low = low + (interval_size * int(cumulative[symbol]) // total)

        # Mirror the encoder's renormalization while consuming new bits.
        while True:
            if high < _HALF:
                pass
            elif low >= _HALF:
                value -= _HALF
                low -= _HALF
                high -= _HALF
            elif low >= _QUARTER and high < _THREE_QUARTERS:
                value -= _QUARTER
                low -= _QUARTER
                high -= _QUARTER
            else:
                break
            low = (low << 1) & _MAX_STATE
            high = ((high << 1) & _MAX_STATE) | 1
            value = ((value << 1) | reader.read_bit()) & _MAX_STATE

    return symbols

docs.title: Custom components
docs.text:
The library is built from small interfaces. This page shows the contract of each one with a minimal working example.

Component Built or called as Must provide Basis basis(in_features, **kwargs) num_components, and one (N, K_c) feature tensor per axis Combiner combiner(basis.num_components, **kwargs) out_features, and (N, out_features) from the features Head head(combiner.out_features, out_features, **kwargs) Any module Loss loss_fn(batch, model) A scalar loss and a dictionary of metrics Metric fn(reconstruction, original) A float Dataset dataset[i] Items with id, input, target, _original; preprocess, postprocess, save Model model(coordinates) (..., in_features) to (..., out_features)

docs.title: A basis
docs.text:
A Gaussian bump basis in a dozen lines:

import torch
from torch import nn
import inro


class GaussianBasis(nn.Module):
    """K Gaussian bumps per axis, centered on a uniform grid over [-1, 1]."""

    def __init__(self, in_features, num_components, width=0.05):
        super().__init__()
        self.in_features = in_features
        self.num_components = [num_components] * in_features
        self.width = width
        self.register_buffer("centers", torch.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, num_components))

    def forward(self, x):  # (N, C) -> C tensors of shape (N, K)
        return tuple(
            torch.exp(-(((x[:, c, None] - self.centers) / self.width) ** 2))
            for c in range(self.in_features)
        )


model = inro.FUTON(
    2, 3,
    basis=(GaussianBasis, {"num_components": 64}),
    combiner=("cp", {"rank": 32}),
    head="linear",
)

A class and a (class, kwargs) pair work anywhere a registry key does, as does a ready module instance. To add a key instead, register the class in inro.models.futon.BASES.

docs.title: A combiner or head
docs.text:
A combiner takes the tuple of per-axis features: tensors, SharedRows on a grid, or Taps for a local basis. A product with a matrix gives a tensor, or SharedRows again on a grid, whose dense() is the matrix. A head is any module, so torch.nn.Linear, inro.MLP, or a class of your own:

class GatedHead(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_features, out_features):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = nn.Linear(in_features, out_features)
        self.gate = nn.Linear(in_features, out_features)

    def forward(self, g):
        return self.linear(g) * torch.sigmoid(self.gate(g))


model = inro.FUTON(
    2, 3,
    basis=("cosine", {"num_components": 128}),
    combiner=("cp", {"rank": 64}),
    head=GatedHead,
)

docs.title: A loss
docs.text:
inro.train calls loss_fn(batch, model) and expects a scalar loss and a dictionary of metrics for the log, as floats or as scalar tensors. Tensors are read only when a step is logged, so the training steps never wait for the GPU in between. batch is the dataset item with its tensors on the training device; keys with a leading underscore stay on the CPU.

A loss that fits only the pixels a mask marks as known:

import torch.nn.functional as F


def masked_mse(batch, model):
    output = model(batch["input"])
    mask = batch["mask"]
    loss = F.mse_loss(output[mask], batch["target"][mask])
    return loss, {"loss": loss.detach()}


train_set = inro.MaskedImageCoordinateDataset(
    "image.png", mask="mask.png", subsample=0.1
)
eval_set = inro.ImageCoordinateDataset("image.png")
result = inro.train(model, train_set, eval_set, loss_fn=masked_mse)

The indexing works before and after subsampling because the dataset flattens input, target and mask with the same indices. inro.rate_distortion_loss and inro.sdf_loss are two more examples of the signature; functools.partial(inro.rate_distortion_loss, alpha=0.01) sets their options.

docs.title: A metric
docs.text:
Metrics are functions fn(reconstruction, original) -> float on whatever the dataset's postprocess returns and its _original holds: uint8 (channels, H, W) images or {0, 1} volumes. Rate metrics take (encoded_bytes, original).

def mae(pred, target):
    return (pred.float() - target.float()).abs().mean().item()


result = inro.train(model, train_set, eval_set, metrics={"psnr": inro.psnr, "mae": mae})

For inro.nerf.evaluate, metrics receive (3, H, W) float images in \([0, 1]\).

docs.title: A dataset
docs.text: A dataset is a torch.utils.data.Dataset whose items carry id, input, target and _original, with preprocess, postprocess and save for the evaluation loop and, optionally, to(device) for GPU-side subsampling. The simplest route is to subclass ImageCoordinateDataset and override what differs; OccupancyCoordinateDataset and MaskedImageCoordinateDataset do exactly that. For a signal with its own geometry, build the coordinates with inro.create_coordinates(size) and follow the conventions.

docs.title: A model
docs.text:
Any module that maps (..., in_features) coordinates in \([-1, 1]\) to (..., out_features) is an INR for the training loop, and, without an output activation, a density network for inro.nerf.RadianceField. inro.MLP accepts a custom layer_class when the novelty is in the layer:

class SoftplusLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_features, out_features, beta=1.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = nn.Linear(in_features, out_features)
        self.beta = beta

    def forward(self, x):
        return F.softplus(self.linear(x), beta=self.beta)


model = inro.MLP(
    2, 3, hidden_features=256, hidden_layers=3,
    layer_class=SoftplusLayer, beta=2.0, output_activation=torch.tanh,
)

Extra keyword arguments go to the hidden layers; the output layer stays linear. SIREN, FINER, Gauss and RealWIRE are built this way and add their initialization after super().__init__().

docs.title: Registries
docs.text:
inro.build_module(spec, registry, *args, **kwargs) is the resolver behind every spec: an instance is returned as is, a key is looked up in registry, a class is called, and a (key_or_class, params) pair adds keyword arguments. A two-element list works too, so specs can come from YAML or JSON. Use it for your own components:

HEADS = {"linear": nn.Linear, "mlp": inro.MLP, "gated": GatedHead}
head = inro.build_module(("gated", {}), HEADS, 64, 3)

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text: Coordinate datasets and their conventions are described on the conventions page.

docs.title: datasets
docs.text:
Image, volume and MRI datasets for implicit neural representations (INRs).

A dataset has length one and ignores the item index. Its item is a dictionary with id, input, target and _original, the reference signal for metrics. Coordinate inputs lie in [-1, 1].

Dataset methods follow load(path, ...), save(x, path, ...), preprocess(x) (raw signal to target) and postprocess(x) (model output to reconstruction). Deep Image Prior uses a fixed noise input instead of coordinates. Super-resolution observes the image through a separable linear degradation, written out by resize_matrix and applied by downsample.

docs.title: ImageCoordinateDataset
docs.text:
ImageCoordinateDataset(image: str | PathLike[str] | Image | Tensor, grid_size: tuple[int, int] | None = None, mode: str = 'RGB', max_samples: int | None = None, subsample: float = 1.0, item_id: str | None = None, seed: int = 0)

Image as coordinate-pixel pairs, with optional random subsampling.

Subsampling flattens input and target to (N, 2) and (N, channels) with shared indices, a new uniformly random subset of the pixels on each access.

Parameters:

  • image (str | PathLike[str] | Image | Tensor) –

    Path, PIL image, or uint8 tensor (channels, H, W).

  • grid_size (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    Size of the coordinate grid; None uses the signal's size. Any other size serves evaluation at that resolution, without subsampling.

  • mode (str, default: 'RGB' ) –

    PIL conversion mode of paths and PIL images; ignored for tensors.

  • max_samples (int | None, default: None ) –

    Cap on the coordinates drawn on each access; None sets no cap.

  • subsample (float, default: 1.0 ) –

    Fraction of the coordinates drawn on each access, in (0, 1].

  • item_id (str | None, default: None ) –

    Item identifier; None uses the path stem, or an empty string without a path.

  • seed (int, default: 0 ) –

    Seed of Python's global RNG; sampling uses PyTorch's and ignores it.

Shape
  • input: (H, W, 2), coordinates in [-1, 1].
  • target: (H, W, channels), pixels in [-1, 1].
  • _original: (channels, H, W), uint8 image.

Examples:

>>> image = torch.zeros(3, 4, 6, dtype=torch.uint8)
>>> item = ImageCoordinateDataset(image)[0]
>>> item["input"].shape, item["target"].shape
(torch.Size([4, 6, 2]), torch.Size([4, 6, 3]))
>>> ImageCoordinateDataset(image, subsample=0.5)[0]["input"].shape
torch.Size([12, 2])
Source code in inro/datasets.py 
def __init__(
    self,
    image: str | os.PathLike[str] | Image.Image | Tensor,
    grid_size: tuple[int, int] | None = None,
    mode: str = "RGB",
    max_samples: int | None = None,
    subsample: float = 1.0,
    item_id: str | None = None,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> None:
    if not 0 < subsample <= 1:
        raise ValueError(f"subsample must be in (0, 1], got {subsample}")
    if max_samples is not None and max_samples <= 0:
        raise ValueError(f"max_samples must be positive, got {max_samples}")

    self.original, self.id = _load_image(image, mode, item_id)
    self.grid_size = grid_size or self.original.shape[1:]
    self.input = self.create_input()
    self.target = self.preprocess(self.original)
    self.subsample = subsample
    self.max_samples = max_samples
    self.seed = seed
    random.seed(self.seed)

def to(self, device: str | torch.device) -> Self:
    """Move the training tensors to ``device`` in place and return self.

    The reference ``original`` stays on the CPU.

    Args:
        device: Device to move them to.
    """
    for name in self._device_attrs:
        value = getattr(self, name, None)
        if isinstance(value, Tensor):
            setattr(self, name, value.to(device))
    return self

@staticmethod
def preprocess(x: Tensor) -> Tensor:
    """Map uint8 pixels to float values in ``[-1, 1]``, channels last.

    Args:
        x: Image ``(channels, H, W)``.

    Returns:
        Target ``(H, W, channels)``.
    """
    x = x.float() * 2 / 255 - 1
    # Contiguous, as a loader's batches are, so that a graph compiled on an item
    # serves them; the moved view keeps the channel stride.
    return x.movedim(0, -1).clone(memory_format=torch.contiguous_format)

    """Map float predictions to uint8 pixels, clamping them to ``[-1, 1]`` first.

    Args:
        x: Predictions ``(H, W, channels)``.

    Returns:
        Image ``(channels, H, W)``.
    """
    x = x.movedim(-1, 0).clamp(-1, 1)
    return ((x + 1) * 255 / 2).round().to(torch.uint8)

Image as coordinate-pixel pairs, with an optional guide image and binary mask.

The preprocessed guide extends the coordinates as extra input channels, and a custom loss can use the mask and its thick boundary. Inputs always use the image resolution. Subsampling flattens every tensor but _original with shared indices.

    Path, PIL image (converted to RGB), or uint8 tensor (channels, H, W).

  • mask (str | PathLike[str] | Image | Tensor | None, default: None ) –

    Binary mask as a path, PIL image (converted to grayscale), or tensor (1, H, W) or (H, W), nonzero values being true; None uses no mask.

    Item identifier; None uses the path stem, or an empty string without a path.

  • seed (int, default: 0 ) –

    Seed of Python's global RNG; sampling uses PyTorch's and ignores it.

Shape

def __init__(
    self,
    image: str | os.PathLike[str] | Image.Image | Tensor,
    side: str | os.PathLike[str] | Image.Image | Tensor | None = None,
    mask: str | os.PathLike[str] | Image.Image | Tensor | None = None,
    subsample: float = 1.0,
    item_id: str | None = None,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> None:
    if not 0 < subsample <= 1:
        raise ValueError(f"subsample must be in (0, 1], got {subsample}")

    self.original, self.id = _load_image(image, "RGB", item_id)
    if side is not None:
        side, _ = _load_image(side, "L", None)
    if mask is not None:
        mask, _ = _load_image(mask, "L", None)

    self.grid_size = self.original.shape[-2:]
    self.input, self.side, self.mask, self.boundary = self.create_input(side, mask)
    self.target = self.preprocess(self.original)
    self.subsample = subsample
    self.seed = seed
    random.seed(self.seed)

def create_input(
    self, side: Tensor | None, mask: Tensor | None
) -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor | None, Tensor | None, Tensor | None]:
    """Return ``(input, side, mask, boundary)`` at the image resolution.

    Args:
        side: Uint8 guide ``(side_channels, H, W)``, or ``None``.
        mask: Mask ``(1, H, W)`` or ``(H, W)``, or ``None``.

    Returns:
        Coordinates with the preprocessed guide appended, that guide, the bool mask
            and its thick boundary; an absent guide or mask gives ``None``.
    """
    coords = create_coordinates(self.grid_size, (-1.0, 1.0))

    if isinstance(side, Tensor):
        side = self.preprocess(side)
        inputs = torch.cat([coords, side], dim=-1)
    else:
        side = None
        inputs = coords

    if isinstance(mask, Tensor):
        mask = mask.squeeze(0).bool()
        boundary = mask_to_boundary(mask, kernel_size=3, mode="thick")
    else:
        mask = None
        boundary = None

    return inputs, side, mask, boundary

docs.text:
SuperResolutionDataset(image: str | PathLike[str] | Image | Tensor, kernels: Sequence[Tensor], num_blocks: int, block_size: int = 8, item_id: str | None = None)

Low-resolution image as blocks of pixels and the coordinates under them.

An INR is fitted to the low-resolution (LR) image through its degradation from high resolution (HR), one matrix per axis. Each access draws B random square blocks of S LR pixels a side, with the global PyTorch RNG, and super_resolution_loss renders their footprints of L HR pixels a side. Neighboring pixels share most of their footprint: at 4x, an 8 x 8 block takes 30 INR evaluations per pixel against 256 for a single pixel.

Parameters:

  • image (str | PathLike[str] | Image | Tensor) –

    LR image as a path, PIL image (converted to RGB), or uint8 tensor (channels, h, w).

  • kernels (Sequence[Tensor]) –

    Degradation matrices (h, H) and (w, W), such as those of resize_matrix. They set the HR grid and the device of the training tensors.

  • num_blocks (int) –

    Blocks B drawn on each access.

  • block_size (int, default: 8 ) –

    LR pixels S on a side of a block.

  • item_id (str | None, default: None ) –

    Item identifier; None uses the path stem, or an empty string without a path.

Shape
  • input: (B, L, L, 2), HR coordinates of each block's footprint.
  • weight_y, weight_x: (B, S, L), kernel rows of each block on its footprint.
  • target: (B, S, S, channels), LR pixels in [-1, 1].
  • _original: (channels, h, w), uint8 LR image.

Examples:

>>> image = torch.zeros(3, 8, 8, dtype=torch.uint8)
>>> kernels = resize_matrix(32, 8), resize_matrix(32, 8)
>>> dataset = SuperResolutionDataset(image, kernels, num_blocks=2, block_size=2)
>>> item = dataset[0]
>>> item["input"].shape, item["weight_y"].shape, item["target"].shape
(torch.Size([2, 20, 20, 2]), torch.Size([2, 2, 20]), torch.Size([2, 2, 2, 3]))
Source code in inro/datasets.py 
def __init__(
    self,
    image: str | os.PathLike[str] | Image.Image | Tensor,
    kernels: Sequence[Tensor],
    num_blocks: int,
    block_size: int = 8,
    item_id: str | None = None,
) -> None:
    device = kernels[0].device
    self.original, self.id = _load_image(image, "RGB", item_id)  # (channels, h, w)
    size = tuple(self.original.shape[1:])
    if tuple(kernel.shape[0] for kernel in kernels) != size:
        raise ValueError(
            f"kernels of {[tuple(k.shape) for k in kernels]} do not map onto "
            f"the {size[0]} x {size[1]} LR image"
        )
    if not 0 < block_size <= min(size):
        raise ValueError(
            f"block_size must be in [1, {min(size)}], got {block_size}"
        )
    self.kernels = list(kernels)
    self.num_blocks, self.block_size = num_blocks, block_size
    self.grid_size = tuple(kernel.shape[1] for kernel in kernels)  # (H, W)
    self.input = self.create_input().to(device)  # HR coordinates, (H, W, 2)
    self.target = self.preprocess(self.original).to(device)  # (h, w, channels)

    # Each kernel row's first tap and one past its last. A block's footprint L is
    # the widest row's span, zeros inside included as at 3x and 5x, plus scale per
    # further row.
    self.first = [(kernel != 0).int().argmax(1) for kernel in kernels]
    ends = [k.shape[1] - (k != 0).flip(1).int().argmax(1) for k in kernels]
    taps = max(int((end - first).max()) for end, first in zip(ends, self.first))
    scale = self.grid_size[0] // self.target.shape[0]
    self.footprint = scale * (block_size - 1) + taps
    if self.footprint > min(self.grid_size):
        raise ValueError(
            f"a block's footprint, {self.footprint} HR pixels, exceeds the "
            f"{self.grid_size[0]} x {self.grid_size[1]} HR grid"
        )

def to(self, device: str | torch.device) -> Self:
    """Move the training tensors and kernels to ``device`` in place and return self.

    The reference ``original`` stays on the CPU.

OccupancyCoordinateDataset(path: str | PathLike[str], resolution: int = 256, grid_size: tuple[int, int, int] | None = None, max_samples: int | None = None, subsample: float = 1.0, item_id: str | None = None, seed: int = 0)

Voxelized shape as coordinate-occupancy pairs.

The shape is centered and scaled into [-0.45, 0.45]^3, as in BACON and FINER. Voxel centers lie at multiples of 1 / resolution, and each holds whether it lies inside the shape; the volume is cropped to its occupied bounds, as in WIRE. A mesh's inside is decided by rays: a center is inside when most of five rays from it cross the surface an odd number of times, which tolerates the small holes of scanned meshes. A point cloud's is the sign of BACON's signed distance. The volume is cached beside the source in .cache/<stem>_<resolution>_centers.pt, which is reused even if the source changes. Subsampling flattens input and target to (N, 3) and (N, 1) with shared indices.

Parameters:

  • path (str | PathLike[str]) –

    .xyz point cloud (columns x y z nx ny nz) or a mesh readable by trimesh.

  • resolution (int, default: 256 ) –

    Voxels per unit length after normalization into [-0.45, 0.45]^3.

  • grid_size (tuple[int, int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    Size of the coordinate grid; None uses the signal's size. Any other size serves evaluation at that resolution, without subsampling.

  • max_samples (int | None, default: None ) –

    Cap on the coordinates drawn on each access; None sets no cap.

  • subsample (float, default: 1.0 ) –

    Fraction of the coordinates drawn on each access, in (0, 1].

  • item_id (str | None, default: None ) –

    Item identifier; None uses the path stem, or an empty string without a path.

  • seed (int, default: 0 ) –

    Seed of Python's global RNG; sampling uses PyTorch's and ignores it.

Shape
  • input: (depth, H, W, 3), coordinates in [-1, 1].
  • target: (depth, H, W, 1), floats in {-1, 1}.
  • _original: (1, depth, H, W), float occupancy in {0, 1}.

Examples:

>>> dataset = OccupancyCoordinateDataset("lucy.ply")
References

Lindell et al., "BACON: Band-limited Coordinate Networks for Multiscale Scene Representation", CVPR 2022. Saragadam et al., "WIRE: Wavelet Implicit Neural Representations", CVPR 2023. Liu et al., "FINER: Flexible Spectral-bias Tuning in Implicit NEural Representation by Variable-periodic Activation Functions", CVPR 2024.

Load, or build and cache, a float occupancy volume.

Meshes need the 3d extra (trimesh reads them, Open3D casts the rays).

Parameters:

def load(self, path: str | os.PathLike[str], resolution: int) -> Tensor:
    """Load, or build and cache, a float occupancy volume.

    Meshes need the ``3d`` extra (trimesh reads them, Open3D casts the rays).

    Args:
        path: ``.xyz`` point cloud (columns ``x y z nx ny nz``) or a mesh readable
            by trimesh.
        resolution: Voxels per unit length after normalization into
            ``[-0.45, 0.45]^3``.

    Returns:
        Occupancy ``(1, depth, H, W)``, cropped to its occupied bounds.
    """
    path = Path(path)
    cache_path = path.parent / ".cache" / f"{path.stem}_{resolution}_centers.pt"
    if cache_path.exists():
        return torch.load(cache_path, weights_only=True).float()

    if path.suffix.lower() == ".xyz":
        vertices, inside = self._point_cloud(path)
    else:
        vertices, inside = self._mesh(path)
    grid = self._voxelize(vertices, inside, resolution)

    cache_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    torch.save(grid, cache_path)
    return grid.float()

Export occupancy as a .dae mesh and a .png render (3d extra).

The render needs no display; where the renderer cannot start, a warning replaces the .png. Its camera is fitted to the grid rather than the mesh, so that reconstructions of one shape are framed alike.

Parameters:

    Occupancy (1, depth, H, W) or (depth, H, W).

  • path (str | PathLike[str]) –

    Output path, whose suffix .dae and .png replace.

  • smooth (bool, default: True ) –

    Whether to apply Gaussian smoothing (sigma 1) before marching cubes at iso-level zero.

  • size (int, default: 1024 ) –

    Side of the square render, in pixels.

  • up (int, default: 1 ) –

    Grid axis drawn upwards; the view looks down the shortest of the other two, which shows the widest silhouette.

  • mesh (bool, default: True ) –

    Whether to write the .dae.

def save(
    self,
    x: Tensor,
    path: str | os.PathLike[str],
    smooth: bool = True,
    size: int = 1024,
    up: int = 1,
    mesh: bool = True,
) -> None:
    """Export occupancy as a ``.dae`` mesh and a ``.png`` render (``3d`` extra).

    The render needs no display; where the renderer cannot start, a warning replaces
    the ``.png``. Its camera is fitted to the grid rather than the mesh, so that
    reconstructions of one shape are framed alike.

    Args:
        x: Occupancy ``(1, depth, H, W)`` or ``(depth, H, W)``.
        path: Output path, whose suffix ``.dae`` and ``.png`` replace.
        smooth: Whether to apply Gaussian smoothing (sigma 1) before marching cubes
            at iso-level zero.
        size: Side of the square render, in pixels.
        up: Grid axis drawn upwards; the view looks down the shortest of the other
            two, which shows the widest silhouette.
        mesh: Whether to write the ``.dae``.
    """
    import mcubes

    # Imported in Jupyter, Open3D enables its web visualizer, which offscreen
    # renders do not use, and announces it.
    os.environ.setdefault("OPEN3D_DISABLE_WEB_VISUALIZER", "true")
    import open3d as o3d

    dae_path = Path(path).with_suffix(".dae")
    png_path = Path(path).with_suffix(".png")

    volume = x.squeeze(0).detach().cpu().numpy()
    if smooth:
        volume = mcubes.smooth(volume.copy(), method="gaussian", sigma=1)

    vertices, triangles = mcubes.marching_cubes(volume, 0)
    if mesh:
        mcubes.export_mesh(vertices, triangles, dae_path)

    geometry = o3d.geometry.TriangleMesh(
        o3d.utility.Vector3dVector(vertices), o3d.utility.Vector3iVector(triangles)
    )
    geometry.compute_vertex_normals()
    material = o3d.visualization.rendering.MaterialRecord()
    material.shader = "defaultLit"
    # Quietly: each renderer announces its EGL context.
    quiet = o3d.utility.VerbosityContextManager(o3d.utility.VerbosityLevel.Warning)
    try:
        with quiet:
            renderer = o3d.visualization.rendering.OffscreenRenderer(size, size)
    except RuntimeError as error:  # a machine without EGL or a GPU
        warnings.warn(f"No renderer ({error}); no {png_path.name}.")
        return
    renderer.scene.add_geometry("mesh", geometry, material)
    renderer.scene.set_background([1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0])
    renderer.scene.show_skybox(False)
    # Tone mapping would gray the white background and flatten the shading.
    renderer.scene.view.set_post_processing(False)
    extent = np.array(volume.shape, dtype=float)
    center = (extent - 1) / 2
    sideways = min({0, 1, 2} - {up}, key=lambda axis: extent[axis])
    across = ({0, 1, 2} - {up, sideways}).pop()
    # Far enough that the grid's nearest face, 4 % larger, fills the 45-degree
    # view along its longer side: a tall shape is never cut at the frame.
    fov = 45.0
    half = 1.04 * max(extent[up], extent[across]) / 2
    distance = half / math.tan(math.radians(fov / 2)) + extent[sideways] / 2
    eye = center + np.eye(3)[sideways] * distance
    renderer.setup_camera(fov, center, eye, np.eye(3)[up])
    o3d.io.write_image(str(png_path), renderer.render_to_image())

@staticmethod
def preprocess(x: Tensor) -> Tensor:
    """Map occupancy in ``{0, 1}`` to float targets in ``{-1, 1}``, channels last.

    Args:
        x: Occupancy ``(1, depth, H, W)``.

def __init__(
    self,
    image: str | os.PathLike[str] | Image.Image | Tensor,
    noise_shape: tuple[int, ...] | None = None,
    noise_channels: int = 16,
    reg_noise_std: float = 1 / 30,
    item_id: str | None = None,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> None:
    self.original, self.id = _load_image(image, "RGB", item_id)
    self.target = self.preprocess(self.original)

    noise_shape = noise_shape or (noise_channels, *self.original.shape[1:])
    generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    self.input = torch.randn(noise_shape, generator=generator) * 0.1

    self.reg_noise_std = reg_noise_std

MRICoordinateDataset(kspace: str | PathLike[str] | Tensor, crop_size: tuple[int, int] | None = None, mask: Tensor | None = None, acceleration: float = 4.0, pattern: Literal['uniform', 'random'] = 'random', center_fraction: float = 0.08, slice_index: int | None = None, item_id: str | None = None, seed: int = 0)

Undersampled multi-coil MRI k-space for coordinate-based reconstruction.

The model predicts interleaved real and imaginary coil images with num_coils * 2 channels. A custom loss pads these to the k-space size, Fourier-transforms them and compares acquired lines against target.

Parameters:

  • kspace (str | PathLike[str] | Tensor) –

    Complex tensor (num_coils, H, W) or fastMRI HDF5 path; a file also provides reconstruction_rss when it has one.

  • crop_size (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    Reconstruction field of view (crop_H, crop_W); None uses the size of the reference RSS image. Required for tensor inputs.

  • mask (Tensor | None, default: None ) –

    Mask of W elements, reshaped to bool (1, 1, W); None generates one.

  • acceleration (float, default: 4.0 ) –

    Target acceleration of the generated mask.

  • pattern (Literal['uniform', 'random'], default: 'random' ) –

    Line pattern of the generated mask, "random" or "uniform".

  • center_fraction (float, default: 0.08 ) –

    Fraction of lines the generated mask keeps at the center.

  • slice_index (int | None, default: None ) –

    Slice of the file to load; None uses the middle one.

  • item_id (str | None, default: None ) –

    Item identifier; None uses the path stem, or an empty string without a path.

  • seed (int, default: 0 ) –

    Seed of the mask's own generator.

Shape
  • input: (crop_H, crop_W, 2), coordinates in [-1, 1].
  • target: (num_coils, H, W), complex masked, normalized k-space.
  • mask: (1, 1, W), bool sampling mask.
  • scale_factor: Scalar normalization factor from preprocess.
  • zero_filled: (crop_H, crop_W), RSS reconstruction in original units.
  • _original: (crop_H, crop_W), reference RSS image, when one is loaded.

Examples:

>>> kspace = torch.randn(2, 8, 8, dtype=torch.complex64)
>>> item = MRICoordinateDataset(kspace, crop_size=(4, 4))[0]
>>> item["input"].shape, item["target"].shape, item["mask"].shape
(torch.Size([4, 4, 2]), torch.Size([2, 8, 8]), torch.Size([1, 1, 8]))
References

Zbontar et al., "fastMRI: An Open Dataset and Benchmarks for Accelerated MRI", arXiv 2018.

def __init__(
    self,
    kspace: str | os.PathLike[str] | Tensor,
    crop_size: tuple[int, int] | None = None,
    mask: Tensor | None = None,
    acceleration: float = 4.0,
    pattern: Literal["uniform", "random"] = "random",
    center_fraction: float = 0.08,
    slice_index: int | None = None,
    item_id: str | None = None,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> None:
    if isinstance(kspace, (str, os.PathLike)):
        self.id = item_id or Path(kspace).stem
        kspace, rss = self.load(kspace, slice_index=slice_index)
    elif isinstance(kspace, Tensor):
        self.id = item_id or ""
        rss = None
    else:
        raise ValueError("kspace must be a str, os.PathLike or Tensor")
    if kspace.ndim != 3 or not kspace.is_complex():
        raise ValueError(
            "kspace must be a complex (num_coils, H, W) tensor, got "
            f"{kspace.dtype} tensor of shape {tuple(kspace.shape)}"
        )

    self.kspace = kspace
    self.num_coils = kspace.shape[0]
    self.kspace_size = tuple(kspace.shape[-2:])
    if not crop_size and rss is None:
        raise ValueError(
            "crop_size must be given when no reconstruction_rss is available "
            "(e.g. for k-space tensor inputs)"
        )
    self.crop_size = crop_size or tuple(rss.shape[-2:])

    if mask is None:
        mask = self.create_undersampling_mask(
            num_cols=kspace.shape[-1],
            acceleration=acceleration,
            pattern=pattern,
            center_fraction=center_fraction,
            seed=seed,
        )
    # Shape (1, 1, W), which broadcasts against k-space (num_coils, H, W).
    self.mask = mask.reshape(1, 1, -1).bool()

    kspace_normalized, self.scale_factor = self.preprocess(
        self.kspace, self.mask, self.crop_size
    )

    self.input = create_coordinates(self.crop_size, (-1.0, 1.0))
    self.target = kspace_normalized * self.mask
    self.original = rss

    self.zero_filled = self.zero_filled_reconstruction(
        kspace, self.mask, self.crop_size
    )

@staticmethod
def load(
    path: str | os.PathLike[str], slice_index: int | None = None
) -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor | None]:
    """Load one fastMRI slice (requires ``h5py``).

    Args:
        path: fastMRI HDF5 file.
        slice_index: Slice of the file to load; ``None`` uses the middle one.

    Returns:
        K-space ``(num_coils, H, W)`` and the reference RSS image
            ``(crop_H, crop_W)``, ``None`` when the file has none.
    """
    import h5py

    with h5py.File(path, "r") as data_file:
        kspace_all = torch.from_numpy(data_file["kspace"][()])
        if slice_index is None:
            slice_index = kspace_all.shape[0] // 2
        rss_target = None
        if "reconstruction_rss" in data_file:
            rss_target = torch.from_numpy(
                data_file["reconstruction_rss"][slice_index]
            )

    return kspace_all[slice_index], rss_target

@staticmethod
def save(x: Tensor, path: str | os.PathLike[str]) -> None:
    """Min-max normalize a magnitude image and save it as an 8-bit PNG.

    Args:
        x: Magnitude image ``(H, W)``.
        path: Output path; ``.png`` is appended if needed.
    """
    image = x.detach().cpu().float()
    image = (image - image.min()) / (image.max() - image.min() + 1e-8)
    _save_png((image * 255).round().to(torch.uint8).unsqueeze(0), path)

create_undersampling_mask(num_cols: int, acceleration: float, pattern: Literal['uniform', 'random'] = 'random', center_fraction: float = 0.08, seed: int = 0) -> Tensor

Return a bool Cartesian sampling mask of shape (num_cols,).

Center lines are always kept. "random" adds lines up to round(num_cols / acceleration) in total, unless the center alone exceeds it. "uniform" adds every round(acceleration)-th line from a random offset, on top of the center.

Parameters:

  • num_cols (int) –

    Number of lines.

  • acceleration (float) –

    Target acceleration of the generated mask.

  • pattern (Literal['uniform', 'random'], default: 'random' ) –

    Line pattern of the generated mask, "random" or "uniform".

  • center_fraction (float, default: 0.08 ) –

    Fraction of lines the generated mask keeps at the center.

  • seed (int, default: 0 ) –

    Seed of the mask's own generator.

@staticmethod
def create_undersampling_mask(
    num_cols: int,
    acceleration: float,
    pattern: Literal["uniform", "random"] = "random",
    center_fraction: float = 0.08,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> Tensor:
    """Return a bool Cartesian sampling mask of shape ``(num_cols,)``.

    Center lines are always kept. ``"random"`` adds lines up to
    ``round(num_cols / acceleration)`` in total, unless the center alone exceeds it.
    ``"uniform"`` adds every ``round(acceleration)``-th line from a random offset,
    on top of the center.

    Args:
        num_cols: Number of lines.
        acceleration: Target acceleration of the generated mask.
        pattern: Line pattern of the generated mask, ``"random"`` or ``"uniform"``.
        center_fraction: Fraction of lines the generated mask keeps at the center.
        seed: Seed of the mask's own generator.
    """
    generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)

    mask = torch.zeros(num_cols, dtype=torch.bool)

    num_center = round(num_cols * center_fraction)
    center_start = (num_cols - num_center) // 2
    mask[center_start : center_start + num_center] = True

    if pattern == "uniform":
        step = round(acceleration)
        offset = torch.randint(0, step, (1,), generator=generator).item()
        mask[offset::step] = True
    elif pattern == "random":
        num_outer = max(round(num_cols / acceleration) - num_center, 0)
        outer_indices = torch.where(~mask)[0]
        permutation = torch.randperm(len(outer_indices), generator=generator)[
            :num_outer
        ]
        mask[outer_indices[permutation]] = True
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown pattern '{pattern}'. Use 'uniform' or 'random'.")

    return mask

zero_filled_reconstruction(kspace: Tensor, mask: Tensor, crop_size: tuple[int, int] | None = None) -> Tensor

Return the RSS magnitude of masked k-space, optionally center-cropped.

The orthonormal inverse FFT is centered: ifftshift before it and fftshift after, which differ for odd sizes.

Parameters:

  • kspace (Tensor) –

    Complex k-space (num_coils, H, W).

  • mask (Tensor) –

    Mask that broadcasts to kspace.

  • crop_size (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    Reconstruction field of view (crop_H, crop_W); None keeps (H, W).

Source code in inro/datasets.py 
@staticmethod
def zero_filled_reconstruction(
    kspace: Tensor, mask: Tensor, crop_size: tuple[int, int] | None = None
) -> Tensor:
    """Return the RSS magnitude of masked k-space, optionally center-cropped.

    The orthonormal inverse FFT is centered: ``ifftshift`` before it and
    ``fftshift`` after, which differ for odd sizes.

    Args:
        kspace: Complex k-space ``(num_coils, H, W)``.
        mask: Mask that broadcasts to ``kspace``.
        crop_size: Reconstruction field of view ``(crop_H, crop_W)``; ``None`` keeps
            ``(H, W)``.
    """
    kspace_masked = kspace * mask

    coil_images = torch.fft.fftshift(
        torch.fft.ifft2(
            torch.fft.ifftshift(kspace_masked, dim=(-2, -1)), norm="ortho"
        ),
        dim=(-2, -1),
    )

    if crop_size is not None:
        height, width = coil_images.shape[-2:]
        crop_height, crop_width = crop_size
        coil_images = coil_images[
            ...,
            (height - crop_height) // 2 : (height + crop_height) // 2,
            (width - crop_width) // 2 : (width + crop_width) // 2,
        ]

    return (coil_images.real**2 + coil_images.imag**2).sum(dim=-3).sqrt()

def preprocess(
    self, x: Tensor, mask: Tensor, crop_size: tuple[int, int], eps: float = 1e-16
) -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor]:
    """Return normalized k-space and its scalar scale factor.

    Divides k-space by the maximum of its masked, cropped zero-filled RSS image. By
    linearity of the FFT, the same scale applies in both domains.

    Args:
        x: Complex k-space ``(num_coils, H, W)``.
        mask: Mask that broadcasts to ``x``.
        crop_size: Reconstruction field of view ``(crop_H, crop_W)``.
        eps: Lower bound of the scale factor.
    """
    zero_filled = self.zero_filled_reconstruction(x, mask, crop_size)
    scale_factor = torch.clamp(zero_filled.max(), min=eps)
    return x / scale_factor, scale_factor

def postprocess(self, x: Tensor) -> Tensor:
    """Convert interleaved coil predictions to RSS magnitude in original units.

    The norm over the last dimension gives the RSS without complex tensors. It is
    clamped to ``[0, 1]``, then multiplied by ``scale_factor``.

    Args:
        x: Predictions ``(crop_H, crop_W, num_coils * 2)``.

    Returns:
        Magnitude ``(crop_H, crop_W)``.
    """
    return torch.clamp(torch.norm(x, dim=-1), min=0.0, max=1.0) * self.scale_factor

def create_coordinates(
    size: tuple[int, ...], domain: tuple[float, float] = (-1.0, 1.0), **kwargs: Any
) -> Tensor:
    """Return an evenly spaced coordinate grid of shape ``(*size, len(size))``.

    Coordinate ``c`` varies along axis ``c``, as with ``indexing="ij"``.

    Args:
        size: Number of points on each axis.
        domain: Endpoints of every axis, both included.
        **kwargs: Passed to ``torch.linspace``, such as ``dtype`` and ``device``.

    Examples:
        >>> create_coordinates((2, 3)).shape
        torch.Size([2, 3, 2])
    """
    axes = [torch.linspace(*domain, length, **kwargs) for length in size]
    return torch.stack(torch.meshgrid(*axes, indexing="ij"), dim=-1)

Extract the boundary of a binary mask by dilation and erosion.

Parameters:

  • mask (Tensor) –

    Binary tensor (H, W), (B, H, W) or (B, 1, H, W).

  • kernel_size (int, default: 3 ) –

    Odd side of the pooling neighborhood.

  • mode (Literal['inner', 'outer', 'thick'], default: 'thick' ) –

    "inner" (mask minus erosion), "outer" (dilation minus mask) or "thick" (dilation minus erosion).

Returns:

  • Tensor –

    Binary boundary with the shape, dtype and device of mask.

Examples:

>>> mask = torch.zeros(5, 5, dtype=torch.bool)
>>> mask[1:4, 1:4] = True
>>> mask_to_boundary(mask, mode="inner").sum().item()
8
Source code in inro/datasets.py 
def mask_to_boundary(
    mask: Tensor,
    kernel_size: int = 3,
    mode: Literal["inner", "outer", "thick"] = "thick",
) -> Tensor:
    """Extract the boundary of a binary mask by dilation and erosion.

    Args:
        mask: Binary tensor ``(H, W)``, ``(B, H, W)`` or ``(B, 1, H, W)``.
        kernel_size: Odd side of the pooling neighborhood.
        mode: ``"inner"`` (mask minus erosion), ``"outer"`` (dilation minus mask) or
            ``"thick"`` (dilation minus erosion).

    Returns:
        Binary boundary with the shape, dtype and device of ``mask``.

    Examples:
        >>> mask = torch.zeros(5, 5, dtype=torch.bool)
        >>> mask[1:4, 1:4] = True
        >>> mask_to_boundary(mask, mode="inner").sum().item()
        8
    """
    original_ndim = mask.ndim
    if mask.ndim == 2:
        mask = mask.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0)
    elif mask.ndim == 3:
        mask = mask.unsqueeze(1)
    elif mask.ndim == 4:
        if mask.shape[1] != 1:
            raise ValueError("mask should be single-channel (C=1) or 2/3-D tensor")
    else:
        raise ValueError("mask must be 2D, 3D (B,H,W), or 4D (B,1,H,W)")

    float_mask = mask.float()
    padding = kernel_size // 2

    dilation = F.max_pool2d(float_mask, kernel_size, stride=1, padding=padding)

    erosion = 1.0 - F.max_pool2d(
        1.0 - float_mask, kernel_size, stride=1, padding=padding
    )

    if mode == "inner":
        boundary = float_mask - erosion
    elif mode == "thick":
        boundary = dilation - erosion
    elif mode == "outer":
        boundary = dilation - float_mask
    else:
        raise ValueError("mode must be 'inner', 'outer' or 'thick'")

    boundary = (boundary > 0.0).to(mask.dtype)

    if original_ndim == 2:
        return boundary[0, 0]
    if original_ndim == 3:
        return boundary[:, 0]
    return boundary

Return the matrix of antialiased bicubic resizing on one axis.

It is the operator of F.interpolate(..., mode="bicubic", antialias=True), whose kernel is that of MATLAB's imresize and PIL's bicubic filter, with which super-resolution benchmarks such as DIV2K make their low-resolution images.

Parameters:

  • size_out (int) –

    Size of the output axis.

  • device (str | device | None, default: None ) –

    Device of the matrix; None uses the default device.

Returns:

    Matrix (size_out, size_in).

>>> kernel = resize_matrix(64, 16)
>>> kernel.shape
torch.Size([16, 64])
>>> (kernel != 0).sum(1).max().item()  # taps of one low-resolution pixel
16

def resize_matrix(
    size_in: int, size_out: int, device: str | torch.device | None = None
) -> Tensor:
    """Return the matrix of antialiased bicubic resizing on one axis.

    It is the operator of ``F.interpolate(..., mode="bicubic", antialias=True)``, whose
    kernel is that of MATLAB's ``imresize`` and PIL's bicubic filter, with which
    super-resolution benchmarks such as DIV2K make their low-resolution images.

    Args:
        size_in: Size of the input axis.
        size_out: Size of the output axis.
        device: Device of the matrix; ``None`` uses the default device.

    Returns:
        Matrix ``(size_out, size_in)``.

    Examples:
        >>> kernel = resize_matrix(64, 16)
        >>> kernel.shape
        torch.Size([16, 64])
        >>> (kernel != 0).sum(1).max().item()  # taps of one low-resolution pixel
        16
    """
    # Resizing the rows of an identity image writes the matrix out, borders included.
    identity = torch.eye(size_in, device=device)[None, None]
    size = (size_out, size_in)
    return F.interpolate(identity, size=size, mode="bicubic", antialias=True)[0, 0]
