docs.title: Related results
docs.text:
The ingredients are classical; the use is in combining them for this model, where every quantity can be computed from the signal and the bound is attained.

  • Matrices. For a matrix, the best rank-\(R\) approximation and its error are the truncated SVD's (Eckart and Young, 1936; Mirsky, 1960), which is item (4).
  • Higher orders. For a tensor of order three or more, a best rank-\(R\) CP approximation need not exist (de Silva and Lim, 2008), which is why item (2) is an infimum and items (3) bracket it.
  • Flattenings. The lower bound is the tail of a matricization, the quantity that bounds the truncation error of the HOSVD (De Lathauwer, De Moor and Vandewalle, 2000) and of the TT-SVD (Oseledets, 2011) from below; the nested SVDs of Lemma 3 are the TT-SVD taken to full rank, with a greedy choice of its heaviest terms in place of a truncation, which for two modes is the Kronecker-product SVD of Van Loan and Pitsianis (1993).
  • Separated representations. The separation rank of a function and its \(\varepsilon\)-rank are the notions of the separated representations of Beylkin and Mohlenkamp (2002, 2005), fitted by alternating least squares; the proposition above says that a fixed basis inherits them up to the truncation.
  • Learning. Learning with CP-structured Fourier coefficients appears in Kargas and Sidiropoulos (2021), with error bounds under smoothness, and with random Fourier features in Wesel and Batselier (2021); their analyses hold in expectation or asymptotically, where the theorem here is an identity for the signal at hand.
  • MLP-based INRs. For MLP-based INRs, the structure of what a network can represent is known (Yüce, Ortiz-Jiménez, Dimitriadis and Frossard, 2022), but no analogue of item (2), the exact error of the best model at a given size, is available.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The whole grid. The theorem needs the signal on its whole grid, since the coefficient tensor is a sum over every sample: it covers representation, not radiance fields or inverse problems, where the signal is observed through a renderer or an operator, and its grid norm says nothing about points off the grid.
  • A linear head. It covers the paper's model, a linear head without bias or output activation; the remark above says what transfers to the benchmarks' heads, and the lower bound does not.
  • Three or more axes. For three or more axes the ceiling falls to the truncation once \(R\) passes the largest \(K_c\), and the certified FUTON trails training by a median 1.06 dB on the volumes, so the bracket is wide there; a tighter lower bound for that regime is open.
  • A conservative certificate. The certified FUTON keeps the heaviest terms of one expansion, and training passes it by a median 0.03 dB on the images and 1.06 dB on the volumes. Item (3) takes any tensor of rank at most \(R\), so a search that improves on those terms, its result taken exactly, tightens the certificate, at the cost of the search.
  • Candidates. The design corollary chooses among the candidate settings it is given; a finer grid of \(K\) and \(R\) costs one bound each.

docs.title: FUTON
docs.text:
FUTON, the Fourier Tensor Network, represents a signal as a truncated series in a fixed basis whose coefficient tensor is kept in low-rank form. This page derives the model, describes each stage as it is implemented, and explains how to size one.

The three stages for one pixel of kodim17. Each array is colored by its entries' sign and size.

docs.title: From a series to a network
docs.text:
Take a signal \(s : [-1, 1]^C \to \mathbb{R}\) and a family of \(K\) functions \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_K\) on \([-1, 1]\). Products of one function per axis form a separable basis of \([-1, 1]^C\), and the signal expands as a generalized Fourier series:

\[ s(\boldsymbol{x}) \approx \sum_{k_1=1}^{K} \cdots \sum_{k_C=1}^{K} \mathcal{W}[k_1, \dots, k_C] \, \prod_{c=1}^{C} \varphi_{k_c}(x_c). \]

Stored in full, the coefficient tensor \(\mathcal{W}\) has \(K^C\) entries: for a \(512 \times 768\) image at the sampling resolution that is the image itself, and for a \(256^3\) volume it is \(16.8\) million coefficients. FUTON's prior is that \(\mathcal{W}\) is compressible, and it stores the tensor in canonical polyadic (CP) form of rank \(R\),

\[ \mathcal{W} = \sum_{r=1}^{R} \boldsymbol{u}^{(1)}_r \circ \cdots \circ \boldsymbol{u}^{(C)}_r , \]

with one factor matrix \(\boldsymbol{U}^{(c)} = [\boldsymbol{u}^{(c)}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{u}^{(c)}_R] \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times R}\) per axis. Substituting the factorization and exchanging the sums turns the \(C\)-fold summation into a product of \(C\) inner products:

\[ \begin{aligned} s(\boldsymbol{x}) &\approx \sum_{r=1}^{R} \prod_{c=1}^{C} \big\langle \boldsymbol{u}^{(c)}_r, \boldsymbol{\varphi}(x_c) \big\rangle \\ &= \boldsymbol{1}^\top \Big( \bigodot_{c=1}^{C} \boldsymbol{U}^{(c)\top} \boldsymbol{\varphi}(x_c) \Big), \end{aligned} \]

where \(\boldsymbol{\varphi}(x_c) = [\varphi_1(x_c), \dots, \varphi_K(x_c)]\) and \(\odot\) is the elementwise product. Nothing in the forward pass is \(K^C\) any more: each axis is projected to \(R\) channels, the channels are multiplied across axes, and the \(R\) products are summed. With \(D\) output channels the final sum becomes a linear map \(\boldsymbol{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times R}\); replacing it with a small MLP gives the model used in the experiments.

The prior holds for natural signals. For kodim23 at \(K = 32\) cosines per axis, \(\mathcal{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{32 \times 32 \times 3}\) holds the image's 3,072 generalized Fourier coefficients, whose energy concentrates at low frequencies: the \(8 \times 8\) lowest carry 78 % of it. A CP tensor of rank 4 keeps the dominant structure in 268 numbers, and the image it represents scores 17.2 dB, against 23.8 dB for all 3,072 coefficients, the most any FUTON with a linear head reaches at this \(K\).

kodim23 and its coefficient tensor in the cosine basis at K = 32 per axis, as an RGB image with one cell per frequency: in full, and at rank 4, the certified FUTON of the error bound, built from the image without training. A channel's coefficient w is shown as 0.5 + 0.5 tanh(w / s), gray at zero, with s the 90th percentile of the full tensor's magnitudes. Each PSNR is that of the image the tensor represents. scripts/futon_coefficients.py computes both.

This is the pipeline head(combiner(basis(x))):

Stage Computes Parameters Keys Basis \(\boldsymbol{\varphi}(x_c)\) per axis none cosine, sinc, legendre, chebyshev, triangle, lanczos Combiner \(\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \bigodot_c \boldsymbol{U}^{(c)\top} \boldsymbol{\varphi}(x_c)\) \(R \sum_c K_c\) cp, tr, tucker Head \(\boldsymbol{V} \boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}) + \boldsymbol{b}\), or an MLP \(RD + D\); one hidden layer adds \(R^2 + R\) linear, mlp, identity 
model = inro.FUTON(
    in_features=3,
    out_features=1,
    basis=("cosine", {"num_components": 128}),
    combiner=("cp", {"rank": 256}),
    head=("mlp", {"hidden_layers": 1, "hidden_features": 128}),
    output_activation=torch.tanh,
)

Each stage accepts a registry key, a (key, kwargs) pair, a module class or a module instance, resolved by inro.build_module. inro.FUTONEncoding holds the basis, built as basis(in_features, **kwargs), and the combiner, built as combiner(basis.num_components, **kwargs); FUTON adds the head, built as head(encoding.out_features, out_features, **kwargs). Custom stages only need to expose num_components (a basis) or out_features (a combiner); see custom components in the API reference.

docs.title: What a point costs
docs.text:
A point costs \(O(R \sum_c K_c)\), linear in the spectral resolution and in the number of axes. A local basis reduces the basis term to its \(2a\) nonzero taps per axis, \(O(aRC)\).

On a grid the projections \(\boldsymbol{U}^{(c)\top} \boldsymbol{\varphi}(x_c)\) are shared, since each depends on one coordinate alone:

Points How the basis is evaluated Cost for \(N\) points Scattered Point by point \(O(NR \sum_c K_c)\) On a grid, \(S_c\) distinct coordinates per axis Each distinct coordinate once, every point gathering its rows \(O(R \sum_c S_c K_c + NCR)\) A grid the batch covers, a head whose first layer is linear The network and that layer as one tensor network over the axes' tables, contracted for the whole grid and read at the points \(O(DR \prod_c S_c)\) for CP, \(D\) the layer's width

The shared path computes the same function and gradients. FUTON takes it whenever every axis of a batch repeats its coordinates, as an image's pixels or any batch drawn from them do. Coordinates that need gradients are always evaluated point by point.

Every combiner is multilinear in the per-axis features, and states its network once, as an einsum equation in which ... stands for the points (combiners). On a grid, a combiner returns its features as GridFeatures, their equation and operands not yet contracted, and giving each axis's ... a subscript of its own makes the network and the head's first linear layer one tensor network. That layer contracts it for the whole grid, in an order planned on the actual sizes, when the grid has at most \(64 / D\) cells per point, \(D\) the layer's width, as a whole image does. That computes the same function too, and spares every point's combined features and the scatter of their gradients, the bulk of a step for the tensor-ring and Tucker combiners.

A basis given grid_size, the sizes of the grid every input lies on, goes one step further: it evaluates its features on that grid once, when it is built, and finds each point's row by rounding. That spares a sort and a GPU synchronization per axis at every batch, and a break in the compiled graph.

A declared grid on scattered points

A point off the declared grid reads its nearest grid point's row, so for scattered inputs a grid trades exactness for speed. The radiance-field benchmark rounds its samples to 2048 points per axis, finer than the ray-marching step, which keeps a trained field's PSNR within a few hundredths of a decibel and renders and trains it in a fraction of the memory.

docs.title: Bases
docs.text:
Six one-dimensional families are implemented. All take num_components, an int for every axis or one count per axis, and normalize.

Four functions of each family on \([-1, 1]\). Cosine, Legendre and Chebyshev are global and indexed by degree; sinc, triangle and Lanczos are shifted kernels indexed by their center. Key \(\varphi_k(x)\) Orthogonal on \([-1, 1]\) Support Smoothness Cardinal cosine \(\cos(k \pi u)\), \(u = (x + 1) / 2\), \(k = 0, \dots, K - 1\) yes global \(C^\infty\) no sinc \(\operatorname{sinc}\big((x - \mu_k) / w\big)\) no global \(C^\infty\) yes legendre \(P_k(x)\), Bonnet's recurrence yes global \(C^\infty\) no chebyshev \(T_k(x)\) under the weight \((1 - x^2)^{-1/2}\) global \(C^\infty\) no triangle \(\max(0, 1 - \lvert x - \mu_k \rvert / w)\) no 2 taps \(C^0\) yes lanczos \(\operatorname{sinc}(t) \operatorname{sinc}(t / a)\) for \(\lvert t \rvert < a\), \(t = (x - \mu_k) / w\) no \(2a\) taps \(C^1\) yes

The kernel families are centered on the uniform grid \(\mu_k = -1 + k w\) with spacing \(w = 2 / (K - 1)\), so the grid of centers is the sampling grid of a signal with \(K\) samples per axis. A cardinal basis satisfies \(\varphi_k(\mu_j) = \delta_{jk}\): each function is one at its own center and zero at all others, so the coefficients of an interpolant are the samples themselves. For sinc this is the Whittaker–Shannon interpolation formula, and Lanczos is its windowed, compactly supported version: with radius \(a\) (radius, default 3, as in the experiments), a coordinate touches only the \(2a\) nearest centers.

Interpolating samples with sinc (top) and Lanczos-3 (bottom) kernels: each sample scales one shifted kernel, and the sum passes through the samples. At one coordinate, all 16 sinc functions are nonzero, but only 6 of the Lanczos-3 functions are.

Normalization shapes the features, and locality how they are stored:

  • normalize (default True) L2-normalizes the feature vector \(\boldsymbol{\varphi}(x_c)\) at each point, not the basis functions. It stabilizes training and is what the experiments use. normalize=False recovers the plain series: exact cardinal interpolation for the cardinal bases, and the TensoRF-CP parameterization for the triangle basis with a CP combiner.
  • Taps. A local basis, triangle or lanczos, returns each axis of scattered points as Taps, only the \(2a\) nonzero features of each coordinate and the column of the first; on a grid, it reads dense tables like any other basis. A product with a factor gathers \(2a\) consecutive rows per coordinate, which torch.compile fuses into one kernel. Taps need a flat batch (N, C); FUTON.forward reshapes for you.

The paper proves that FUTON with the cosine basis is a universal approximator. In practice the choice of family barely moves accuracy on the grid, and moves training time a lot; the basis ablation measures both.

docs.title: Combiners
docs.text:
Key Computes Output width Parameters cp \(\bigodot_c \boldsymbol{U}^{(c)\top} \boldsymbol{\varphi}(x_c)\) rank \(R \sum_c K_c\) tr \(\operatorname{vec}\big(\prod_c \mathcal{G}^{(c)} \times_2 \boldsymbol{\varphi}(x_c)\big)\) with cores \(\mathcal{G}^{(c)} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times K_c \times r}\) \(r^2\) \(r^2 \sum_c K_c\) tucker The projections contracted with a core \(\max_c r_c\) \(\sum_c K_c r_c + \prod_c r_c \cdot \max_c r_c\)
  • CPCombiner is the paper's model: factors[c] holds \(\boldsymbol{U}^{(c)}\), shape (K_c, rank), initialized Kaiming-uniform with fan-in \(K_c\).
  • TRCombiner chains tensor-ring cores into an \(r \times r\) matrix per point and flattens it, leaving the closure of the ring to the head. A ring of rank \(r\) has the size of a CP combiner of rank \(r^2\).
  • TuckerCombiner projects each axis to its own rank and contracts the projections with a core, so with a linear head the weight tensor is in Tucker format; CP is the case of a superdiagonal core.

Each combiner is an einsum equation over the projections of the axes, with ... for the points: on two axes, ...r,...r->...r for CP, ...ab,...bc->...ac for the ring, and ...b,abz,...a->...z for Tucker, whose largest-rank projection comes first. Per point, FUTON contracts the operands in the order they are listed; on a grid, it gives every ... its own subscript and contracts the network with the output projection in one planned einsum.

A combiner's output on a grid, GridFeatures, behaves as its features would: torch.nn.functional.linear, which a linear head and the first layer of an mlp head call, contracts it together with the layer's weight, and every other torch function takes the features themselves, GridFeatures.dense().

The combiner ablation finds CP the most accurate at equal size, 0.4 dB above the ring and 2.5 dB above Tucker, though on a grid both of them train faster.

docs.title: Heads
docs.text:
• linear is nn.Linear(R, D): \(\hat{s}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{V} \boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}) + \boldsymbol{b}\). With it, FUTON is exactly a rank-\(R\) CP model of the signal in the chosen basis, Eq. (9) of the paper, and its capacity is the capacity of that tensor format. The occupancy benchmark uses it: on volumes at 256 voxels per unit length it tied the best MLP at equal size, in a seventh of the training time.
  • identity passes the combiner's features on.
  • mlp is inro.MLP(R, D, hidden_layers=h), a ReLU network whose hidden width defaults to \(R\). The other benchmarks use one hidden layer. The nonlinearity lets the model represent more than a rank-\(R\) tensor at the same size: on images it is worth about 8 dB over a linear head of the same size (head ablation).

output_activation is applied last; the benchmark models use torch.tanh to match targets in \([-1, 1]\). Inside a RadianceField, the density network must have no output activation, since the field applies its own.

docs.title: Sizing a model
docs.text:
With a CP combiner and a one-hidden-layer MLP head of width \(M\) (hidden_features, \(R\) by default), the parameter count is

\[ R \sum_{c=1}^{C} K_c \;+\; (RM + M) \;+\; (MD + D), \]

and with a linear head, \(R \sum_c K_c + RD + D\).

Each task chooses FUTON's components per axis and head as every baseline's settings are chosen, on the data the baselines were tuned on: the best quality at a training time and memory that stay low. The rank is the largest multiple of 5 that keeps FUTON smaller than every baseline of the task. The benchmarks run FUTON with the cosine basis at these sizes:

Task num_components rank Head Parameters Images, \(512 \times 768\) Kodak [H // 2, W // 2] 280 MLP, 1 hidden layer of width 64 197,379 Occupancy, voxel grids of 154 to 461 per side [D // 2, H // 2, W // 2] 215 to 310 by shape Linear 128,786 to 131,441 Radiance fields, density network with 16 outputs 100, read from a table of 2048 points per axis 180 MLP, 1 hidden layer of width 64 66,624 (73,027 with the color network)

Rules of thumb from the ablations

num_components is the bandwidth. Half the resolution per axis, \(K = N/2\), is the best of \(N/4\), \(N/2\) and \(N\) on images and volumes. On radiance fields, whose \(N\) is the 200 pixels of a view, \(N/4\) edges ahead of it, by about 0.1 dB on the validation views, because the MLP head recovers what the coarser basis loses, but at a larger rank and more memory.

Spend a budget on rank first. At a fixed budget the rank matters more than extra components, so spend a larger budget on \(R\) before \(K\).

With PyTorch's default Adam, these learning rates work:

Basis Images Volumes Radiance fields cosine 1e-1 3e-2 1e-2

The other five bases take 3e-2 on images in the basis ablation.

docs.title: Relation to the paper
docs.text: The cosine basis, CP combiner and linear head implement Eq. (9) of the paper: encoding.combiner.factors[c] stores \(\boldsymbol{U}^{(c)}\) and head.weight stores \(\boldsymbol{V}\). Coordinates are mapped internally from \([-1, 1]\) to \([0, 1]\). The implementation drops the paper's \(\sqrt{2}\) factor on the cosines and normalizes the feature vectors by default; normalize=False recovers Eq. (1) up to per-frequency constants that the factors absorb. The other bases, the tensor-ring and Tucker combiners and the MLP head are extensions; the benchmarks use the cosine basis, with a one-layer MLP head on images and radiance fields and a linear head on volumes.

docs.title: INRs in Inro
docs.text:
An implicit neural representation (INR) represents a signal as a parametric function of its coordinates, fitted to samples of the signal by minimizing a reconstruction loss.

\[ \hat{s}_\theta : [-1, 1]^C \to \mathbb{R}^D \]

a signal x₁, x₂ INR FUTON, SIREN, ... value R, G, B

Signal Coordinates Values Image a pixel, in \([-1, 1]^2\) \(D = 3\), its color Occupancy volume a voxel, in \([-1, 1]^3\) \(D = 1\), inside or outside Radiance field a position and a view direction a density and a color

Inro keeps this abstraction explicit: models are modules on coordinates, datasets are coordinate/value pairs, and one training loop serves every task that fits samples directly.

flowchart TB
    datasets["<b>Datasets</b><br/>coordinates and targets"] --> train["<b>inro.train</b><br/>one loop"]
    models["<b>Models</b><br/>FUTON, SIREN, InstantNGP, ..."] --> train
    losses["<b>Losses</b>"] -.-> train
    train --> evaluate["<b>inro.evaluate</b><br/>chunked_inference"]
    evaluate --> metrics["<b>Metrics</b><br/>psnr, ssim, lpips, iou, ..."]
    models --> field["<b>inro.nerf</b><br/>RadianceField, renderers, train, evaluate"]

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Every model maps a tensor of coordinates (..., in_features) in \([-1, 1]\) to values (..., out_features), so it can be called on a single point, a batch or a whole grid:

model = inro.FUTON(
    2, 3, basis=("cosine", {"num_components": 64}), combiner=("cp", {"rank": 32}), head="linear"
)
model(torch.rand(10, 2) * 2 - 1).shape      # (10, 3)
model(torch.rand(4, 5, 2) * 2 - 1).shape    # (4, 5, 3)

The constructors share in_features, out_features and, where they apply, hidden_features, hidden_layers and output_activation. The model zoo lists them all.

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text:
A dataset yields dictionaries with four keys:

Key Content id A name for the signal, used in logs and file names input Coordinates to evaluate the model at target The values to fit, in the model's output range _original The reference signal in its native form, used by the metrics; keys with a leading underscore stay on the CPU

ImageCoordinateDataset and OccupancyCoordinateDataset follow this scheme; the conventions page tabulates their shapes.

  • One signal, one item. len(dataset) == 1, and random subsampling happens on access: with subsample=0.1, every dataset[0] returns a fresh random tenth of the coordinates and their values, flattened.
  • Benchmarks. The occupancy benchmark trains this way, on \(2^{20}\) fresh voxels per step; the image benchmark takes the whole image at every step.
  • Helpers. preprocess maps native values to targets, postprocess maps model output back, save writes a reconstruction to disk, and to(device) moves the training tensors so that subsampling runs on the GPU.

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
inro.train(model, train_dataset, eval_dataset, **options) fits a model in place.

  1. Draw a batchthe whole signal or a random subset
  2. Compute the lossloss_fn(batch, model)
  3. StepAdam under a cosine schedule
  4. Log and evaluateevery few steps, off the clock
Part What it does Options Optimizer Adam. Every benchmark trains every model with PyTorch's defaults, (0.9, 0.999) and 1e-8, so that the optimizer favors none of them lr, weight_decay, adam_betas, adam_eps Schedule Steps of one batch each, with CosineAnnealingLR down to lr / 100 num_steps Loss loss_fn(batch, model) -> (loss, metrics); by default the mean squared error, logging the PSNR for targets in \([-1, 1]\) loss_fn Evaluation inro.evaluate reconstructs each item in chunks, maps the output through postprocess, and calls each metric as fn(reconstruction, original) eval_interval, metrics, chunk_size Logging Records the training metrics of the step's batch, printed above a progress bar, and writes log.txt, log.json, each evaluation's reconstruction and checkpoint.pt log_interval, log_dir, ckpt_path

The return value is {"config", "model_dict", "history"}: the run's settings, the final parameters, and one record per logged step with elapsed, the seconds spent training so far, the training metrics of the step's batch and, when the step was evaluated, the mean evaluation metrics under "eval". The records are plain dictionaries, so pd.DataFrame(result["history"]) gives a learning curve.

docs.title: Evaluation and inference
docs.text:
• inro.evaluate(model, dataset, metrics=...) runs the evaluation half of the loop on its own, for example on a checkpoint (ckpt_path) or on another grid than the one trained on.
  • inro.chunked_inference(model, coordinates, chunk_size=...) evaluates a model on any coordinate tensor under torch.no_grad(), flattening the leading dimensions for chunking and restoring them afterwards.

docs.title: Radiance fields
docs.text: Novel view synthesis does not fit samples of the signal directly: the supervision is posed images, and the INR is queried along rays. inro.nerf therefore has its own dataset (BlenderDataset), field (RadianceField, which wraps any model from the zoo as its density network), renderers, and train and evaluate functions with the same shape of return value. The radiance field tutorial covers them.

docs.title: The model zoo
docs.text:
Twelve architectures share one interface: Model(in_features, out_features, ...) maps coordinates (..., in_features) in \([-1, 1]\) to (..., out_features). They are re-implementations under one training loop, at settings taken from the authors' code, and the benchmarks compare them at equal parameter counts.

  • FUTON

    A fixed basis per axis, a low-rank combiner across axes, and a head.

  • Coordinate networks

    MLPs whose prior sits in the first layer or in the activation: RFF, PE-MLP, SIREN, Gauss, WIRE, FINER, MFN.

  • Grid and tensor models

    Learnable feature grids and factorizations: Instant-NGP, TensoRF, GA-Planes, F-INR.

docs.title: FUTON
docs.text:
Model Class Idea Reference FUTON FUTON A fixed basis per axis, a low-rank CP combiner across axes, and a linear or MLP head Ashtari et al., arXiv 2026

The benchmarks run it with its default basis, the cosine, as FUTON in the results and the configs; the basis ablation compares the sinc and Lanczos bases and three more with it. The FUTON page explains every part.

docs.title: Coordinate networks
docs.text:
MLPs whose prior sits in the first layer or in the activation.

Model Class Idea Reference RFF RFF Random Fourier features \([\sin(2\pi \boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{x}), \cos(2\pi \boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{x})]\), \(\boldsymbol{B} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\), then a ReLU MLP Tancik et al., NeurIPS 2020 PE-MLP PEMLP NeRF's positional encoding \([\boldsymbol{x}, \sin(2^k \boldsymbol{x}), \cos(2^k \boldsymbol{x})]\), then a ReLU MLP Mildenhall et al., ECCV 2020 SIREN SIREN Sine layers \(\sin(\omega (\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{b}))\) with SIREN initialization Sitzmann et al., NeurIPS 2020 Gauss Gauss Gaussian layers \(\exp(-(s (\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{b}))^2)\) Ramasinghe and Lucey, ECCV 2022 WIRE WIRE, RealWIRE Complex, or real, Gabor wavelet layers \(\cos(\omega z_1) \exp(-(s z_2)^2)\) Saragadam et al., CVPR 2023 FINER FINER Variable-periodic sines \(\sin(\omega (\lvert z \rvert + 1) z)\) Liu et al., CVPR 2024 MFN MFN Multiplicative Gabor filter network: each stage multiplies a Gabor filter of the coordinates into the hidden state Fathony et al., ICLR 2021
  • FreSh (Kania et al., ICLR 2025) is not an architecture but a choice of SIREN's first-layer frequency: inro.fresh_select picks it per signal, before training, as the candidate whose untrained output has the spectrum nearest the signal's, and inro.SIREN(first_omega=...) takes it, its later layers keeping omega.
  • MLP underlies most of them: a plain ReLU network by default, or a network of custom layers (layer_class=inro.SineLayer, inro.GaussLayer, inro.FinerLayer, inro.RealGaborLayer) with their own activations.
  • WIRE is the complex-valued network of the paper. The experiments use RealWIRE, the real Gabor variant from the same paper and code, which trains about 1.5× faster at equal parameter count and has real weights.

docs.title: Grid and tensor models
docs.text:
Learnable feature grids, read by interpolation and decoded by a ReLU MLP, and a factorization into one network per axis.

Model Class Idea Reference Instant-NGP InstantNGP, HashEncoding Multiresolution hash encoding (16 levels, 2 features per level by default) and a bias-free ReLU MLP, mirroring tiny-cuda-nn Müller et al., SIGGRAPH 2022 TensoRF TensoRF Factorized grids: CP (products of line grids) or VM (line-plane products, 3D) Chen et al., ECCV 2022 GA-Planes GAPlanes, MultiVector, FeatureGrid Line, plane and volume grids combined by an expression such as "[e1 o e2, e12]" Sivgin et al., ICML 2025 F-INR FINR One SIREN per coordinate, its outputs combined per channel by a CP or tensor-train decomposition, with no decoder Vemuri et al., WACV 2026

FeatureGrid is the building block: a learnable grid of any dimension sampled with align_corners=True on \([-1, 1]\). MultiVector combines several with elementwise products, sums and concatenation, and GAPlanes and TensoRF add the decoder.

docs.title: Shared conventions
docs.text: Topic Rule Widths and depths hidden_features is the hidden width and hidden_layers the number of hidden layers, so hidden_layers=h means h + 1 weight layers (MFN: h Gabor filters, h - 1 hidden linear layers and one output layer). WIRE and RealWIRE divide the nominal width by \(\sqrt{2}\) to keep the parameter count comparable to real networks Output activations Every model takes output_activation, a callable applied last. The benchmarks use torch.tanh for targets in \([-1, 1]\) and none inside a RadianceField Equal capacity inro.count_parameters(model, trainable_only=False) is how the configs were matched. The image models hold 197k to 209k parameters, the occupancy models about 132k, and the NeRF density networks about 68k (75k with the shared color network) Learning rates Each model has its own, the best of {3e-1, 1e-1, 3e-2, 1e-2, 3e-3, 1e-3, 3e-4, 1e-4} on two signals of the task, as each config's header says

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
The paper's experiments are one protocol applied to three tasks, documented in enough detail to rerun them.

  • Benchmarks

    Every model's size, costs and final metrics on all three tasks, with convergence plots and qualitative comparisons.

  • Ablations

    FUTON's basis, bandwidth, rank, combiner and head, varied one at a time on images.

  • Reproducing the paper

    The data, the training scripts and their configs, and the run directories that hold every result.

docs.title: The protocol at a glance
docs.text:
Task Signals Budget Steps One step sees Schedule Scored on Images 24 Kodak images about 197k 1000 the whole image cosine, to a hundredth all pixels Occupancy 5 Stanford shapes about 131k 1000 \(2^{20}\) random voxels cosine, to a hundredth all voxels Radiance fields 8 Blender scenes about 74k, its color network included 25,000 4096 rays exponential, to a tenth (torch-ngp's recipe) all 200 test views

Every model of a task follows the same rules:

  • Hyperparameters. Those of its authors' code, wherever the budget allows them.
  • FUTON's size. Its components per axis and head are chosen per task on the data its baselines were tuned on: half the resolution and 64 units on images and radiance fields, where FUTON reads its basis from a table of 2048 points per axis, and half the resolution and a linear head on volumes. Its CP rank is the largest multiple of 5 that keeps it smaller than every baseline. The bandwidth and head ablations show the choice on images.
  • Learning rate. From the grid {3e-1, 1e-1, 3e-2, 1e-2, 3e-3, 1e-3, 3e-4, 1e-4}, chosen on two signals of the task; on volumes, a rate that leaves some shape empty, every voxel outside, is passed over.
  • Optimizer. PyTorch's default Adam.
  • Run. Seed 0 on an NVIDIA A100, the model compiled with torch.compile in a warm-up pass that keeps compilation out of the clock.
  • Costs. From the same runs: the training time counts the training steps alone, every evaluation records how long it took and its peak memory, and every training step its own peak. Each cost in the tables is the median over the signals of a task, so a run slowed by other work on its GPU does not move it.
  • Metrics. On the full signal, LPIPS with its VGG network. The tables report the mean over the signals of a task with a within-signal standard error (a plain one for IoU, which saturates on every shape), the best value in bold and the second in italics.

docs.title: Ablations
docs.text:
FUTON's design choices, varied one at a time on the image task: the basis, the bandwidth at a fixed size, the rank on either side of that size, the combiner and the head.

Basis

37.6 dB

The cosine basis leads, the sinc basis follows at 37.4 dB, and all six families cost the same to train.

Bandwidth

K = N / 2

At a fixed size, halving or doubling it costs 0.7 to 1.1 dB.

Rank

+3.4 to 5.0 dB

Per doubling, from a quarter to four times the benchmark's rank.

Combiner

CP leads

It beats the tensor ring and Tucker by 0.4 and 2.5 dB; on a grid both train faster, in 3.7 and 2.0 s against 4.2 s.

Head

−7.4 dB

The cost of a linear head at equal size; a wider MLP takes two to three times as long.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
Default model The benchmark's FUTON: \(K = (H/2, W/2)\) components per axis, 384 × 256 for a landscape image, CP rank 280 and a one-layer MLP head 64 wide, 197,379 parameters, trained at 1e-1 Setting The benchmark's: the 24 Kodak images at 768 × 512, 1000 steps, each on the whole image, compiled and timed as the benchmark's on A100s, so only the model changes Size Every model but the rank study's takes the largest rank, a multiple of 5, that keeps FUTON smaller than every baseline (F-INR (SIREN), 198,806 parameters) Learning rate The default's, 1e-1, with three exceptions that each section names: the five families beside the cosine take the sinc basis's rate, 3e-2; two models of the sweeps take 3e-2 because it wins on kodim01 and kodim17, as the benchmark picks its rates; and the Tucker combiner takes 3e-2 because 1e-1 diverges Tables The benchmark's columns: every cost is the median over the images, bold marks the best value in a column and italics the second, and ± is one within-image standard error Configs configs/ablation-futon/

The default model appears in every study. The bandwidth and rank studies reuse the benchmark's runs of it, at 37.63 dB; the other three run it again, so that each stands alone, and land at 37.62 to 37.63 dB, the run-to-run variation of one model and seed.

docs.title: Basis
docs.text:
All six families at the default size, so that the parameter count does not depend on the basis: the columns are what each family costs and what it buys. The cosine basis trains at its own rate, 1e-1, and the other five at the sinc basis's, 3e-2, the benchmark's rate for it.

PSNR against training time for every basis, the band one within-image standard error.
  • Orthogonal, global and smooth: the cosine, Legendre's polynomials and Chebyshev's, the last under a weight.
  • Global and smooth, not orthogonal: the sinc.
  • Compact support: the triangle (\(C^0\)) and Lanczos (\(C^1\)) kernels.

The benchmark's cosine basis leads at 37.63 dB, ahead on 22 of the 24 images, the sinc follows 0.20 dB behind it, then Lanczos at 36.97 dB and Chebyshev, Legendre and the triangle at 36.0 to 36.4.

Basis #Params (k) Training time (s) ↓ Training memory (MB) ↓ Inference throughput (MPix/s) ↑ Inference memory (MB) ↓ PSNR (dB) ↑ SSIM ↑ LPIPS ↓ Cosine 197.4 4.2 359 230.4 201 37.63 ± 0.49 0.955 ± 0.001 0.098 ± 0.002 Chebyshev 197.4 4.1 359 230.3 201 36.44 ± 0.16 0.939 ± 0.001 0.124 ± 0.002 Legendre 197.4 4.2 360 210.4 201 36.29 ± 0.12 0.937 ± 0.001 0.129 ± 0.001 Triangle 197.4 4.1 359 242.6 201 36.03 ± 0.10 0.934 ± 0.001 0.126 ± 0.001 Lanczos 197.4 4.1 359 223.4 201 36.97 ± 0.09 0.944 ± 0.001 0.112 ± 0.001 Sinc 197.4 4.1 359 248.4 201 37.43 ± 0.09 0.949 ± 0.001 0.108 ± 0.001
  • Accuracy. Among the orthogonal families the cosine leads the two polynomial ones by 1.2 and 1.3 dB, and among the kernels Lanczos's smoother lobes beat the triangle's kinks by 0.9 dB, on every image.
  • Cost. Training costs the same for every family, 4.1 to 4.2 s and 359 to 360 MB: each basis is tabulated on the pixel grid (grid_size = (H, W)), so a step contracts tables of the same shape whatever the family, and the compact support of the triangle and Lanczos saves nothing there. Evaluation runs at 210 to 248 megapixels per second, within the spread of the default model from one study to the next, 204 to 249.
  • Other metrics. SSIM and LPIPS order the bases as PSNR does, but for the triangle and Legendre, 0.26 dB apart, which LPIPS swaps.

docs.title: Bandwidth
docs.text:
The relative bandwidth \(\kappa = K / N\), the components per axis as a fraction of the pixels, over {1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2}, at the budget. A rank costs a factor entry per component on each axis and a weight per hidden unit, \((K_1 + K_2 + 64) R + 259\) parameters in all, so the rank falls as the bandwidth grows: 885, 515, 280, 145 and 75. At \(\kappa = 1\) each axis has as many components as pixels, the grid's Nyquist rate, and \(\kappa = 1/2\) is the benchmark's FUTON. The model at \(\kappa = 1/8\) trains at 3e-2, since at 1e-1 it loses 1.4 dB on kodim01 and kodim17.

PSNR against the relative bandwidth at the budget, the band one within-image standard error; the ring marks the benchmark's model.

Half the resolution is best, at 37.63 dB, ahead of each other bandwidth on 23 of the 24 images, and the PSNR falls on either side: by 0.67 dB at \(\kappa = 1/4\) and 1.07 dB at \(\kappa = 1\), and by 4.2 and 5.4 dB at 1/8 and 2.

  • Below \(\kappa = 1/2\) the rank grows but the basis is coarser than the image's detail, which the MLP's nonlinearity only partly makes up: at \(\kappa = 1/8\) the cosines alone cap a linear FUTON at 23.65 dB on average, the truncation on the error bound page, and the MLP reaches 33.41.
  • Above it the rank shrinks, and past \(\kappa = 1\) the extra components add no function the pixel grid can tell apart, so \(\kappa = 2\) pays twice the factor entries for the span of \(\kappa = 1\).
κ R #Params (k) Training time (s) ↓ Training memory (MB) ↓ Inference throughput (MPix/s) ↑ Inference memory (MB) ↓ PSNR (dB) ↑ SSIM ↑ LPIPS ↓ 1/8 885 198.5 9.0 442 111.9 219 33.41 ± 0.15 0.914 ± 0.003 0.167 ± 0.004 1/4 515 198.0 6.1 392 156.9 201 36.95 ± 0.18 0.948 ± 0.003 0.118 ± 0.004 1/2 280 197.4 4.1 359 228.7 201 37.63 ± 0.51 0.955 ± 0.003 0.098 ± 0.003 1 145 195.1 2.8 341 254.1 201 36.56 ± 0.19 0.936 ± 0.002 0.140 ± 0.003 2 75 197.1 2.2 331 335.5 201 32.26 ± 0.26 0.860 ± 0.007 0.271 ± 0.008

The costs run the other way, since the rank sets them: at \(\kappa = 1/8\) FUTON trains 2.2 times slower than at 1/2, at 1.2 times the memory, and at \(\kappa = 2\) in half the time, for 5.4 dB less. SSIM and LPIPS agree with the PSNR's order.

docs.title: Rank
docs.text:
The CP rank over {70, 140, 280, 560, 1120} at the benchmark's bandwidth, \(\kappa = 1/2\), on either side of the budget: the size doubles with the rank, from 49,539 to 788,739 parameters, a quarter to four times the benchmark's. Rank 1120 trains at 3e-2, since at 1e-1 it loses 4.6 dB on kodim01 and kodim17.

PSNR against the CP rank at \(\kappa = 1/2\), the band one within-image standard error; the ring marks the benchmark's model.

Rank keeps paying. Each doubling adds 3.4 to 5.0 dB, the last, to rank 1120, still 3.8: there FUTON holds 788,739 parameters, two thirds of the image's 1,179,648 values, and reaches 46.33 dB, still 12.6 dB below the 58.9 dB of the images' 8-bit quantization.

In the benchmark, the budget rather than the model holds FUTON near 38 dB.

R #Params (k) Training time (s) ↓ Training memory (MB) ↓ Inference throughput (MPix/s) ↑ Inference memory (MB) ↓ PSNR (dB) ↑ SSIM ↑ LPIPS ↓ 70 49.5 2.2 330 305.8 201 30.81 ± 0.28 0.826 ± 0.010 0.304 ± 0.008 140 98.8 2.7 340 249.8 201 34.20 ± 0.29 0.903 ± 0.003 0.190 ± 0.004 280 197.4 4.1 359 228.7 201 37.63 ± 0.46 0.955 ± 0.003 0.098 ± 0.003 560 394.5 6.2 398 152.0 201 42.58 ± 0.20 0.983 ± 0.005 0.040 ± 0.004 1120 788.7 10.9 473 95.2 251 46.33 ± 0.30 0.992 ± 0.005 0.016 ± 0.005

The costs grow slower than the rank: from 280 to 1120, training takes 2.6 times as long at 1.3 times the memory, and evaluation runs 2.4 times slower. Below the benchmark's rank the fixed costs show, and halving the rank saves only a third of the training time.

docs.title: Combiner
docs.text:
Tensor-ring and Tucker combiners against the CP one, at the default \(K\), each at the largest rank within the budget.

  • Tensor ring. A ring of rank \(r\) feeds the head \(r^2\) features and grows with them: rank 16 holds 180,483 parameters, and rank 17 would hold 203,715. It trains at the default's rate, 1e-1.
  • Tucker. It takes a rank per axis in proportion to its components, \(R_c = \gamma K_c\) with \(\gamma = 0.163\): on a 512 × 768 image it projects the axes to 41 and 62 directions and contracts them with a \(41 \times 62 \times 62\) core whose 62 features feed the head, 196,135 parameters. It trains at 3e-2, since at 1e-1 it diverges on 8 of the 24 images.
PSNR against training time for every combiner, the band one within-image standard error.

CP is the most accurate, ahead of both on 23 of the 24 images, but on a grid no longer the cheapest: each combiner reads the whole image off one contraction, which costs the more the wider the bonds it sums over, CP's 280 ranks, the ring's \(16 \times 16\) or Tucker's 62.

  • Against the ring it gains 0.36 dB, in 1.1 times the ring's training time and the same memory.
  • Against Tucker it gains 2.51 dB, in twice Tucker's training time: the core holds 157,604 of Tucker's parameters, while each axis passes through only 41 or 62 directions against CP's 280.
Combiner #Params (k) Training time (s) ↓ Training memory (MB) ↓ Inference throughput (MPix/s) ↑ Inference memory (MB) ↓ PSNR (dB) ↑ SSIM ↑ LPIPS ↓ CP 197.4 4.2 359 203.5 201 37.62 ± 0.41 0.955 ± 0.001 0.098 ± 0.002 TR 180.5 3.7 356 216.9 201 37.26 ± 0.27 0.947 ± 0.001 0.112 ± 0.002 Tucker 196.1 2.0 330 325.3 201 35.12 ± 0.16 0.915 ± 0.002 0.170 ± 0.003

docs.title: Head
docs.text:
With a linear head FUTON is exactly a rank-\(R\) CP model of the signal's coefficients in its basis, the model the theory treats; the benchmark on images uses a one-layer MLP 64 wide. Wider MLPs and the linear head are compared at equal size, each at the largest rank within the budget: 255 behind a hidden layer of 128 units, 220 behind 256, and 305 for the linear map, which frees the MLP's 18k parameters. All four keep the tanh on the output and the default's rate, 1e-1.

PSNR against training time for every head, the band one within-image standard error.
  • Width buys little at this size: the 128- and 256-wide MLPs give up rank for it and end 0.54 and 0.33 dB above the 64-wide one on average, but above it on only 12 and 6 of the 24 images, in 1.9 and 2.8 times its training time and 2.9 and 3.3 times its memory.
  • A natural image is far from a low-rank tensor in a smooth basis: at equal size the linear head stops at 30.26 dB, 7.4 dB below the MLP, though it trains fastest, in a third of the MLP's time.

The MLP head 64 wide is the default on images, the cheapest of the three widths, and the linear head remains the model to reason about: without its bias and tanh, it is the model the error bound covers. Occupancy volumes differ: on grids of 256 voxels per unit length the linear head tied the best MLP at equal size, in a seventh of its training time, so the volumes' benchmark uses it.

Head #Params (k) Training time (s) ↓ Training memory (MB) ↓ Inference throughput (MPix/s) ↑ Inference memory (MB) ↓ PSNR (dB) ↑ SSIM ↑ LPIPS ↓ MLP, 64 wide (R = 280) 197.4 4.2 359 248.6 201 37.62 ± 0.49 0.955 ± 0.002 0.098 ± 0.003 MLP, 128 wide (R = 255) 196.4 8.1 1024 131.7 602 38.16 ± 0.15 0.954 ± 0.002 0.099 ± 0.001 MLP, 256 wide (R = 220) 198.1 12.0 1176 90.4 749 37.95 ± 0.17 0.951 ± 0.002 0.106 ± 0.002 Linear (R = 305) 196.1 1.4 37 346.1 19 30.26 ± 0.27 0.874 ± 0.006 0.201 ± 0.005

docs.text:
Thirteen models on three tasks, at equal parameter count per task.

Images, Kodak

+0.90 dB

FUTON, 37.63 dB, against MFN's 36.72, in 4.1 s against 57.3 s.

docs.title: Reading the numbers
docs.text:
AccuracyTraining speedInference
  • Images. FUTON leads PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS, by 0.90 dB over MFN, the strongest baseline, and is ahead of every baseline on 21 of the 24 images.
  • Volumes. It has the best mean IoU, 99.90 % against 99.69 % for GA-Planes, and the best IoU on every shape. It passes 99 % on every shape after 2.1 s of training on average, against 4.0 s for Instant-NGP, 23 s for GA-Planes and 24 s for RFF, the only other models to pass it on every shape.
  • Radiance fields. It leads FINER by 0.60 dB and five of the eight scenes.
  • The fastest. FUTON is the fastest model to train on volumes, in 5.4 s against Instant-NGP's 9.4 s, and Instant-NGP on images and radiance fields: 3.6 s against FUTON's 4.1 s and 147 s against 152 s.
  • FUTON's place. It follows Instant-NGP closely on images and radiance fields and leads it on volumes: 99 % IoU on every shape in 2.1 s on average against 4.0 s, and 99.90 % against 99.58 % at the end.
  • Memory. FUTON's training memory is the lowest on every task: 0.36 GB on images, 0.28 GB on volumes and 1.88 GB on radiance fields.
  • Implementations. The hash grid is a PyTorch port of tiny-cuda-nn's, without the fused CUDA kernels, gathering every level in one batched pass; FUTON is plain PyTorch, and every model is compiled.
  • Images and volumes. FUTON is the fastest on both: 229 megapixels per second against Instant-NGP's 198 on images, and 537 megavoxels per second against TensoRF's 202 on volumes.
  • Radiance fields. A radiance field renders a whole view in one pass in 20 to 30 ms, 34 to 50 frames per second, and FUTON is the fastest, at 49.6 against 47.2 for TensoRF, 45.7 for GA-Planes and 44.0 for Instant-NGP.
  • Memory. FUTON infers in the least memory on images, 201 MB, and on volumes, 0.61 GB against TensoRF's 1.19 GB; it renders a radiance field in the least, 2.04 GB, which TensoRF and GA-Planes match: nearly all of that is the ray marcher's buffers for the view's 40,000 rays.

docs.title: How to read the tables
docs.text:
The tables come from the runs' results.json, and the figures are the paper's.

  • Marks. Bold marks the best value in a column and italics the second.
  • Errors. ± is one standard error over the signals, after removing each signal's own level (a paired standard error). IoU, which saturates near 100 % on every shape, takes the plain standard error over the shapes.
  • Costs. Accuracy and costs come from the same runs. Every model is compiled with torch.compile and trained on an A100 after an untimed warm-up pass that compiles it. The training time counts the training steps alone; inference throughput and memory are the medians over a run's evaluations, for a radiance field over its 200 test views, each rendered whole in one pass, and training memory is the run's peak. Each cost in the tables and figures is the median over a task's signals.
Notes on the rows
  • A name in parentheses is the variant a row runs where its kind has several: the backbone of F-INR and FreSh. FUTON runs its default basis, the cosine; the basis ablation compares it with five others.
  • TensoRF is the variant its authors recommend for the dimension: CP on images (the only one in 2D) and VM on volumes and radiance fields; both are in the configs.
  • MFN is the GaborNet of the two networks of its paper, and WIRE the real Gabor variant (inro.RealWIRE) from the WIRE paper and code.
  • F-INR (SIREN) gives each coordinate its own SIREN, built and initialized as in its authors' image code, and combines them per channel by a CP decomposition. Their settings do not fit the budget, so we tuned at equal size what they leave open: the split between width and rank (in 2D the most rank a width allows, one more than the width; width 96 and rank 259 on volumes, width 32 and rank 39 on radiance fields), the first layer's frequency (200 on images, above their 100, and 100 elsewhere) and the decomposition, CP rather than the tensor train they pick for shapes and radiance fields. Neither the positional encoding of their image experiments nor the SIREN of their shape code helps at this size. Their paper fits radiance fields with per-axis hash grids; here the axes are SIRENs on every task.
  • FreSh (SIREN) is the SIREN row with its first-layer frequency chosen per signal before training, by matching the spectrum of the untrained network's output to the signal's, and the search counts toward its training time. Its paper covers images and radiance fields; on volumes it reads the 3D spectrum of the occupancy grid, our adaptation.

docs.title: Checks against the literature
docs.text:
Where the protocol meets a published one, the numbers agree, allowing for the shorter radiance-field schedule.

  • Radiance fields. The protocol is FINER's, which trains for 37,500 steps; at our 25,000 and our 75k budget, SIREN lands 0.3 dB and FINER 0.6 dB below that paper's table on average, by at most 1.1 dB on a scene, and our PE-MLP and WIRE are stronger than its.
  • Hash grid. Its low radiance-field score is what a 75k budget leaves it: its tables hold \(2^{11}\) entries per level, 256 times fewer than in its paper.

The ablations take FUTON apart, and Reproducing the paper has the commands that produced every number above.

docs.title: Reproducing the paper
docs.text:
Every number of the paper comes from the scripts in scripts/. This page is the full pipeline, from an empty data/ folder to the runs in logs/.

The scripts and configs live in the repository, so start from a clone: git clone https://github.com/pashtari/inro.git, then pip install -e ".[3d,nerf]".

  1. 1. Datascripts/download_*.py → data/
  2. 2. Trainingscripts/train_*.py → logs/
  3. 3. Ablationsconfigs/ablation-futon/ → logs/
  4. 4. Analysesscripts/futon_*.py → logs/
  5. 5. Resultslogs/**/results.json

docs.title: 1. Data
docs.text:
python scripts/download_kodak.py      # data/Kodak/, 24 images, about 30 MB
python scripts/download_meshes.py     # data/occupancy/, 5 meshes, about 3 GB
python scripts/download_blender.py    # data/nerf/blender/, 8 scenes, about 2.4 GB

The Kodak images come from Rich Franzen's mirror, the meshes from the Stanford 3D Scanning Repository (rotated into canonical pose where a release is not), and the Blender scenes from a pinned Hugging Face mirror of the official Google Drive release. All three scripts resume and keep existing files.

docs.title: 2. Training
docs.text:
scripts/train_<task>.py fits every model of configs/<task>.yaml to every signal of the task:

python scripts/train_image.py --compile            # 24 images x 13 models -> logs/image/<image>/<model>/
python scripts/train_occupancy.py --compile        # 5 shapes x 14 models  -> logs/occupancy/<shape>/<model>/
python scripts/train_nerf.py --compile             # 8 scenes x 14 models  -> logs/nerf/<scene>/<model>/

The three scripts share one command line:

Option Meaning --data PATH ... Signals to fit; default: every signal under data/ for the task --models NAME ... Model names from the config; default: all --config FILE ... Configs, deep-merged in order; the last names the log directory (configs/<name>.yaml writes to logs/<name>/) --set KEY.PATH=VALUE ... Override one value, read as YAML, e.g. train.num_steps=500 or models.SIREN.train.lr=3e-4 --log-dir DIR Where the runs go --overwrite Rerun runs that already finished --compile Compile each model with torch.compile before its warm-up pass, as every run of the paper was --device DEV cuda when available, else cpu

A config holds the shared data and train settings and, per model, its Inro class, constructor kwargs and training overrides (the learning rate). Image configs may use expressions in the image height H and width W, such as [H // 2, W // 2], and the occupancy config in the voxel grid's D, H and W, where FUTON's entry names a parameter budget whose largest CP rank the script fills in. Each config's header says how its learning rates were chosen, and # deviation marks a setting that departs from the authors' published ones.

Finished runs are skipped, so an interrupted sweep restarts where it stopped, and a failed run writes error.txt and lets the sweep continue. Runs are keyed by model name, so a variant needs its own name or its own --log-dir:

python scripts/train_image.py --models Gauss --overwrite                       # rerun one model in place
python scripts/train_image.py --set models.SIREN.train.lr=0.001 --log-dir logs/siren-lr
python scripts/train_image.py --config configs/ablation-futon/basis.yaml       # -> logs/ablation-futon/basis/
What a run directory holds

log.txt, log.json, checkpoint.pt, the final reconstruction (images) or two rendered test views (NeRF), and results.json with the training configuration, the model's setup from the YAML, num_params, train_time, the final metrics (NeRF: the mean over the 200 test views, with every view under test_views), the history, and the provenance: the commit, PyTorch version and GPU of the run. The commits are those of the development history, which the release squashes; every run's configuration is the released config's. Occupancy runs write no mesh, since rendering needs EGL and a GPU driver.

Measured on A100s (1000 steps; NeRF 25,000), each signal's models in one job:

Task Per model Per signal Whole sweep Images 56 s 13 min 5.2 h Occupancy 98 s 23 min 1.9 h NeRF 5 min 77 min 10 h

A run's time includes compiling its model and its 20 evaluations, with LPIPS on images; training alone takes from 3 s (Instant-NGP) to a minute (MFN) on an image. Every run uses seed 0; some GPU kernels accumulate in a nondeterministic order, so a rerun on the same hardware lands within about a tenth of a decibel of a run, and training times vary with the machine and its load.

docs.title: 3. Ablations
docs.text:
The FUTON ablations are configs in configs/ablation-futon/, run through the image script. All keep the benchmark's settings (the 24 Kodak images, 1000 steps on the whole image), so only the model changes, and all but the basis study run the cosine basis alone:

Config Models Varies basis.yaml 6 The six bases at the benchmark's size bandwidth.yaml 5 The relative bandwidth \(\kappa = K / N\) over {1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2}, each at the largest rank, a multiple of 5, within the budget rank.yaml 5 The CP rank over {70, 140, 280, 560, 1120} at \(\kappa = 1/2\), 49,539 to 788,739 parameters tensor_net.yaml 3 Tensor-ring and Tucker combiners against CP head.yaml 4 MLP heads 64, 128 and 256 wide and the linear head, at equal size 
for study in basis bandwidth rank tensor_net head; do
  python scripts/train_image.py --config configs/ablation-futon/$study.yaml --compile
done
Runs that are shared between experiments

Runs that another experiment already holds are copied rather than repeated, each copy's results.json naming its source: the default model of the bandwidth and rank studies, for one, is the benchmark's FUTON.

docs.title: 4. Analyses
docs.text:
Two scripts study FUTON itself, from the signals rather than from trained runs:

python scripts/futon_coefficients.py  # kodim23's coefficient tensor at K = 32, in full and at rank 4 -> logs/coefficients/
python scripts/futon_bound.py         # the error bound against Adam, on the 24 images and 5 volumes -> logs/bound/

The first computes the tensor of the FUTON page's figure in seconds on a CPU, without training: the image's generalized Fourier coefficients in full, and the certified FUTON at each rank (--image, --components and --ranks choose others). The second runs the error bound's experiment, which trains each of its settings once with Adam to compare.

docs.title: 5. Results
docs.text:
Every run's results.json holds its metrics and costs, so the runs can be read directly:

import json
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

records = [json.loads(p.read_text()) for p in Path("logs").rglob("results.json")]
table = pd.json_normalize(records)

The tables aggregate them as follows:

  • Errors. The ± in the tables is a paired standard error over the signals: each signal's own level is removed before the error is taken, which is the uncertainty of a comparison between models rather than of an absolute level; IoU, which saturates near 100 % on every shape, takes the plain standard error over the shapes. A band in a figure spans one of them, the same error.
  • Costs. They come from the benchmark runs themselves: the training time counts the training steps alone, after a warm-up pass that compiles the model, and every evaluation records how long it took and its peak memory. Each cost in the tables is the median over a task's signals, so a run slowed by other work on its GPU does not move it.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
From an empty environment to a trained INR in two short pages.

  • Installation

    Requirements, the optional extras, and the benchmark data.

  • Your first INR

    Fit FUTON to an image, read the result, and swap in another model.

docs.title: The package at a glance
docs.text:
Everything is importable from the top-level package:

import inro

inro.FUTON, inro.SIREN, inro.InstantNGP                       # models
inro.ImageCoordinateDataset, inro.OccupancyCoordinateDataset  # datasets
inro.train, inro.evaluate, inro.chunked_inference             # training and evaluation
inro.psnr, inro.ssim, inro.lpips, inro.iou                    # metrics
inro.futon_bound                                              # FUTON's error bound
inro.nerf                                                     # radiance fields

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Python 3.11 or newer and PyTorch 2.10 or newer, with or without CUDA. Everything runs on the CPU; a GPU makes training practical.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
From PyPIWith the extrasFrom source 
pip install inro

pip install "inro[3d,nerf]"

For the training scripts, configs and notebooks, which live in the repository:

git clone https://github.com/pashtari/inro.git
cd inro
pip install -e ".[3d,nerf,dev]"

Check the install:

import torch, inro

print(inro.__version__, torch.cuda.is_available())

PyTorch and the NVIDIA driver

pip install inro brings PyTorch's default build from PyPI, which is made for a recent CUDA release and uses the GPU only with a driver that supports it. If the check prints False on a machine with a GPU, install the PyTorch build that matches the driver first, as pytorch.org shows, and inro after it:

nvidia-smi  # the newest CUDA version the driver supports, top right
pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu126  # drivers for CUDA 12.6 or newer
pip install inro

docs.title: Extras
docs.text:
Extra Installs Needed for 3d PyMCubes, pycollada, trimesh, Open3D Meshes as occupancy volumes, and exporting and rendering reconstructed meshes nerf nerfacc, imageio CUDA occupancy-grid ray marching, and writing novel-view videos dev black, pytest, pyinstrument Formatting, the test suite and profiling docs mkdocs-material, mkdocs-glightbox, mkdocstrings Building this site

nerfacc and the CUDA toolkit

nerfacc compiles a CUDA extension the first time it is used and needs a CUDA toolkit for that. Without one, inro.nerf.is_nerfacc_available() is False and inro.nerf.create_renderer() falls back to the built-in PyTorch renderer, which produces the same images more slowly.

docs.title: Benchmark data
docs.text:
The experiments use three public datasets. The scripts, in the repository, download them into data/, which is ignored by git.

Dataset Script Content Size Subset Kodak scripts/download_kodak.py 24 images, 768 × 512 about 30 MB --images 1 17 23 Stanford scripts/download_meshes.py 5 meshes about 3 GB --meshes armadillo thai_statue Blender scripts/download_blender.py 8 NeRF synthetic scenes about 2.4 GB --scenes lego ship

Each script also takes --output-dir and --force. Interrupted downloads resume, and existing files are kept. The layout is what the training scripts and notebooks expect:

data/
├── Kodak/kodim01.png ... kodim24.png
├── occupancy/armadillo.ply  dragon.ply  happy_buddha.ply  lucy.ply  thai_statue.ply
└── nerf/blender/<scene>/transforms_{train,val,test}.json + images

Occupancy volumes are voxelized on first use and cached beside the mesh in data/occupancy/.cache/<name>_<resolution>_centers.pt.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
From a clone of the repository:

pip install -e ".[dev]"
black --check inro tests scripts  # formatting, line length 88
pytest -q                         # tests that need CUDA or local data skip themselves

docs.title: Your first INR
docs.text:
Fit FUTON to one image, read what the training loop returns, and swap in another model. Any RGB image works; the code below uses a Kodak image from the installation page.

  1. Datasetan image as coordinates and values
  2. Modela function of coordinates
  3. TrainingAdam with cosine annealing
  4. Inferenceevaluate it anywhere

docs.title: Fit an image
docs.text:
import torch
import inro

image = "data/Kodak/kodim19.png"
dataset = inro.ImageCoordinateDataset(image)  # (1)!
H, W, _ = dataset.target.shape

model = inro.FUTON(  # (2)!
    in_features=2,
    out_features=3,
    basis=("cosine", {"num_components": [H // 2, W // 2]}),
    combiner=("cp", {"rank": 280}),
    head=("mlp", {"hidden_layers": 1, "hidden_features": 64}),
    output_activation=torch.tanh,  # (3)!
)

result = inro.train(  # (4)!
    model,
    dataset,
    dataset,
    num_steps=1000,
    lr=1e-1,
    metrics={"psnr": inro.psnr, "ssim": inro.ssim},
    log_interval=250,
    eval_interval=250,
)
print(result["history"][-1]["eval"])
  1. dataset.input holds the pixel-center coordinates, (H, W, 2) in \([-1, 1]\), and dataset.target the RGB values, (H, W, 3), also in \([-1, 1]\). Each access returns the whole image; subsample=0.1 would draw a fresh random 10 % of the pixels per access instead, flattened to (N, 2) and (N, 3).
  2. Three specs, each a registry key, a (key, kwargs) pair, a class or a module instance. The cosine basis has half as many functions per axis as the image has pixels, the CP combiner has rank 280, and the head is an MLP with one hidden layer of width 64, whose first layer reads a batch that covers the image off the whole grid in one contraction.
  3. The targets are in \([-1, 1]\), and so is the output of tanh.
  4. Adam with cosine annealing from lr down to lr / 100, one optimizer step per batch; this dataset's one item is the whole image, so every step sees every pixel. Every log_interval steps it prints the training metrics above a progress bar. Every eval_interval steps, and at the last, it maps predictions back to uint8 with dataset.postprocess and adds the metrics to that line.

On a GPU this takes about a dozen seconds (13 s on an RTX 4060 Ti) and ends near 37.8 dB PSNR.

This is the benchmark's FUTON

It holds 197,379 parameters. The benchmark also tabulates the basis on the pixel grid (grid_size) and compiles the model, which trains it in about 4 s on an A100.

The result is a plain dictionary:

result["config"]       # seed, device, model, num_params, optimizer settings, ...
result["model_dict"]   # the final state dict
result["history"][-1]  # {"step": 1000, "elapsed": ..., "mse": ..., "psnr": ...,
                       #  "eval": {"psnr": ..., "ssim": ...}}

docs.title: Reconstruct and save
docs.text:
To rebuild the image, evaluate the model on the dataset's coordinate grid in chunks and map the output back to pixels:

output = inro.chunked_inference(model, dataset.input, chunk_size=65536)  # (H, W, 3) in [-1, 1]
reconstruction = dataset.postprocess(output.cpu())                       # uint8 (3, H, W)

print(inro.psnr(reconstruction, dataset.original))
dataset.save(reconstruction, "kodim19_futon.png")

Coordinates need not lie on the pixel grid: inro.create_coordinates((2 * H, 2 * W)) gives a twice-finer grid on the same domain, and model(coords) evaluates the continuous representation there. How well it interpolates depends on the basis and on num_components; see FUTON.

docs.title: Log to disk
docs.text:
Pass log_dir to keep a record of the run:

result = inro.train(model, dataset, dataset, num_steps=1000, lr=1e-1, log_dir="logs/quickstart")
File Content log.txt The console's lines, with the run's configuration log.json The same records as JSON, read back with inro.read_json_records checkpoint.pt The final state dict kodim19_reconstructed.png The evaluation's reconstruction

docs.title: Swap the model
docs.text:
Every model in the zoo takes in_features and out_features first and maps (..., in_features) coordinates in \([-1, 1]\) to (..., out_features) values, so the training call does not change:

model = inro.SIREN(2, 3, hidden_features=256, hidden_layers=4, output_activation=torch.tanh)
result = inro.train(model, dataset, dataset, num_steps=1000, lr=1e-3, metrics={"psnr": inro.psnr})

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
