    The benchmark's models and learning rates, with learning curves.

  • Occupancy volumes

    The same loop on a 3D shape, scored by IoU.

  • Radiance fields

    Any model as the density network of a NeRF.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Each tutorial is a complete, runnable workflow for one task, at the benchmarks' settings.

  • Fitting an image

    FUTON and the baselines on a Kodak image, with learning curves.

    Needs an image.

  • Occupancy volumes

    A 3D shape as an INR on \([-1, 1]^3\), scored by IoU and exported as a mesh.

    Needs a mesh and the 3d extra.

  • Radiance fields

    Any model as the density network of a NeRF, trained on posed views and rendered in orbit.

    Needs a Blender scene.

  • Notebooks

    Three notebooks that run one signal end to end, with every plot.

    Needs the data.

docs.title: Fitting an image
docs.text:
The image task fits an INR \([-1, 1]^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3\) to one image and scores it on every pixel. This tutorial follows configs/image.yaml and scripts/train_image.py, so what you run here is what the benchmark ran.

kodim19 at about 197k parameters: every featured model's reconstruction with its PSNR over the whole image, and two regions magnified beneath it.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
import torch
import inro

path = "data/Kodak/kodim19.png"
train_set = inro.ImageCoordinateDataset(path)  # the whole image at every step
eval_set = inro.ImageCoordinateDataset(path)
H, W = eval_set.grid_size

Each access is one training step, and the benchmark trains on the whole image at every step, as the papers of the SIREN family do. Other options:

Option Effect subsample Draws a fresh random share of the pixels instead max_samples Caps the draw, for images too large for one step mode="L" Loads a grayscale image (out_features=1) item_id Names the signal in logs when you pass a tensor or PIL image instead of a path

docs.title: Models at equal size
docs.text:
Each benchmark model holds about 197k parameters. FUTON's basis size follows the image, half the sampling resolution per axis, and its grid_size declares the pixel grid, on which the basis is evaluated once and each point reads its row. The first layer of its MLP head reads a batch that covers the image off the grid in one contraction.

FUTONSIRENFINERInstant-NGPTensoRF 
futon = inro.FUTON(
    2, 3,
    basis=("cosine", {"num_components": [H // 2, W // 2], "grid_size": (H, W)}),
    combiner=("cp", {"rank": 280}),
    head=("mlp", {"hidden_layers": 1, "hidden_features": 64}),
    output_activation=torch.tanh,
)

siren = inro.SIREN(2, 3, hidden_features=256, hidden_layers=4, omega=30.0,
                   output_activation=torch.tanh)

finer = inro.FINER(2, 3, hidden_features=256, hidden_layers=4, omega=30.0,
                   output_activation=torch.tanh)

ngp = inro.InstantNGP(
    2, 3,
    num_levels=20, features_per_level=2, log2_hashmap_size=13,
    base_resolution=16, max_resolution=max(H, W) // 2,
    hidden_features=64, hidden_layers=2, output_activation=torch.tanh,
)

tensorf = inro.TensoRF(2, 3, rank=176, resolution=256, mode="cp",
                       hidden_features=256, hidden_layers=2,
                       output_activation=torch.tanh)

The learning rate matters. Every model trains with PyTorch's default Adam, at these rates:

Model FUTON SIREN FINER Instant-NGP TensoRF Learning rate 1e-1 1e-3 1e-3 3e-2 3e-2

configs/image.yaml lists all thirteen models with their rates and, where a setting departs from the authors' code, a comment saying why. Use inro.count_parameters(model, trainable_only=False) when you change a size.

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
result = inro.train(
    futon,
    train_set,
    eval_set,
    num_steps=1000,
    lr=1e-1,
    metrics={"psnr": inro.psnr, "ssim": inro.ssim, "ms_ssim": inro.ms_ssim, "lpips": inro.lpips},
    log_interval=50,
    eval_interval=50,
    log_dir="logs/tutorial/kodim19/FUTON",
)

The metrics run on the uint8 reconstruction against the original every 50 steps.

Tip

LPIPS is the slow one, since it runs a VGG network each time. Leave it out of metrics while iterating, and compute it once at the end with inro.evaluate.

docs.title: Learning curves
docs.text:
history is a list of records, one per logged step, with the evaluation metrics under "eval":

import pandas as pd

curve = pd.DataFrame(
    {"step": h["step"], "time": h["elapsed"], **h["eval"]}
    for h in result["history"] if "eval" in h
)
curve.plot(x="time", y="psnr")
The same curve over the 24 Kodak images, for FUTON and the strongest model of each family.

inro.LinePlot wraps seaborn for the multi-model case: collect one record per model and step and call LinePlot(records).plot(x="time", y="psnr", hue="model"). The notebook notebooks/image_representation.ipynb collects such records for six models and draws them with seaborn itself.

docs.title: Reconstruction
docs.text:
output = inro.chunked_inference(futon, eval_set.input, chunk_size=65536)  # (H, W, 3)
image = eval_set.postprocess(output.cpu())                                # uint8 (3, H, W)
eval_set.save(image, "kodim19_futon.png")

inro.evaluate(model, eval_set, metrics=..., ckpt_path="logs/.../checkpoint.pt", log_dir=...) does the same from a checkpoint and writes the reconstruction beside the logs.

docs.title: The benchmark script
docs.text:
scripts/train_image.py runs every model of the config on every image under data/Kodak/, writes each run to logs/image/<image>/<model>/, and skips runs that already have a results.json:

python scripts/train_image.py                                        # all images, all models
python scripts/train_image.py --data data/Kodak/kodim19.png --models FUTON SIREN
python scripts/train_image.py --set train.num_steps=500 --log-dir logs/short

Sizes in the config may be expressions in the image height H and width W, such as max(H, W) // 2. See Reproducing the paper for the full command-line interface.

docs.title: Radiance fields
docs.text:
inro.nerf turns any model of the zoo into the density network of a radiance field, trains it on posed images by volume rendering, and scores held-out views. The protocol is FINER's, which is torch-ngp's Blender recipe: 200 × 200 views, 25 training views, scored on all 200 test views, here trained for 25,000 steps instead of 37,500. This follows configs/nerf.yaml and scripts/train_nerf.py.

The lego scene rendered in orbit by SIREN, Instant-NGP and FUTON at equal parameter count (about 75k), with the test-view PSNR.
  1. Raysfrom posed views
  2. Samplesalong each ray, in an occupancy grid
  3. Density networkany model of the zoo
  4. Color networkfeatures and view direction
  5. Volume renderinga pixel, against the target

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
import torch
import inro

root = "data/nerf/blender/lego"
train_set = inro.nerf.BlenderDataset(root, split="train", downsample=4, skip=4)
val_set = inro.nerf.BlenderDataset(root, split="val", downsample=4)
test_set = inro.nerf.BlenderDataset(root, split="test", downsample=4)
  • downsample=4 reduces the 800 × 800 renders to 200 × 200 by area averaging, and skip=4 keeps 25 of the 100 training views.
  • Camera positions are scaled by scene_scale=0.8 into the box [-bound, bound]^3 with bound=1, marching starts at near=0.2, and the background is white.
  • dataset[i] returns a full view's rays and RGBA, and sample_rays draws random rays across views for training without materializing a ray buffer.

docs.title: Field and renderer
docs.text:
field = inro.nerf.RadianceField(
    density_net=(inro.FUTON, {  # (1)!
        "basis": ("cosine", {"num_components": 100, "grid_size": 2048}),  # (2)!
        "combiner": ("cp", {"rank": 180}),
        "head": ("mlp", {"hidden_layers": 1, "hidden_features": 64}),
    }),
    color_net=("mlp", {"hidden_features": 64, "hidden_layers": 2}),  # (3)!
    geometry_features=15,
    direction_encoding="sh",
    aabb=train_set.aabb,
)
renderer = inro.nerf.create_renderer(aabb=train_set.aabb, near=train_set.near, far=train_set.far)
  1. Receives in_features=3 and out_features=1 + geometry_features: one density logit and 15 features, on positions mapped from the scene box to \([-1, 1]^3\). The field applies trunc_exp to the density, so the network has no output activation.
  2. Samples along rays lie on no grid, so FUTON's basis would be evaluated at every one of them. grid_size=2048 reads it from a table of 2048 points per axis instead, each coordinate rounded to the nearest, 0.001 apart and finer than the marching step, which keeps a trained field's PSNR within a few hundredths of a decibel and renders and trains it in a fraction of the memory.
  3. Maps the features and the encoded view direction to RGB ("sh": 16 real spherical harmonics, as in Instant-NGP; "identity": raw directions, as in FINER). The field applies a sigmoid, so it has no output activation either.

Every model in the benchmark shares this color network and renderer; only the density network changes, so the comparison is between spatial representations.

create_renderer picks nerfacc when its CUDA extension works and the pure-PyTorch renderer otherwise. Both march rays through an occupancy grid (grid_resolution=128, updated every 16 steps) with a step of \(\sqrt{3} \cdot \text{extent} / 1024\) and at most max_samples_per_ray=1024 occupied samples.

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
result = inro.nerf.train(
    field,
    renderer,
    train_set,
    eval_dataset=val_set,
    eval_indices=[0, 25, 50, 75],
    num_steps=25000,
    num_rays=4096,
    lr=1e-2,
    eval_interval=2500,
    log_dir="logs/tutorial/lego/FUTON",
)

Each step updates the occupancy grid, renders 4096 random training rays, composites predictions and targets onto a random background color, and takes an Adam step, with PyTorch's default settings and the learning rate decaying exponentially to lr / 10. A run of 25,000 steps takes FUTON a few minutes on an A100.

Output Content history step, elapsed, loss, the training psnr and num_samples every log_interval steps, and the mean validation metrics under "eval" every eval_interval log_dir The field's checkpoint.pt and renderer.pt, the renderer's state with its occupancy grid: load both to render a saved run as it was scored

Learning rates in configs/nerf.yaml range from 3e-4 (SIREN, FINER) to 3e-2 (Instant-NGP, TensoRF-VM, GA-Planes), with FUTON at 1e-2.

docs.title: Evaluation and rendering
docs.text:
scores = inro.nerf.evaluate(field, renderer, test_set)  # PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS on all 200 views
print(scores["mean"])

scores["views"] holds one record per view with its index, render time and metrics; return_images=True adds the rendered (H, W, 3) images; indices selects a subset. metrics accepts any fn(pred, target) on (3, H, W) images in \([0, 1]\).

To render new viewpoints, build camera-to-world poses and call render_views:

import imageio.v2 as imageio

poses = [inro.nerf.pose_spherical(theta, -30.0, train_set.radius) for theta in range(0, 360, 12)]
frames = inro.nerf.render_views(field, renderer, test_set, poses)  # list of (H, W, 3) uint8 arrays
imageio.mimsave("lego_orbit.gif", frames, duration=0.083, loop=0)

render_image(field, renderer, rays_o, rays_d) renders arbitrary rays, returning RGB, opacity and depth.

docs.title: The benchmark script
docs.text:
scripts/train_nerf.py trains every model of the config on every scene under data/nerf/blender/, evaluates on the 200 test views, each rendered whole in one pass, and saves two rendered test views per run. The NeRF sweep is the long one: about five minutes per model and scene on an A100, 112 runs in all.

python scripts/train_nerf.py --data data/nerf/blender/lego --models FUTON

docs.title: Notebooks
docs.text:
Three notebooks in notebooks/ run one signal end to end, one per task. They are the interactive version of the training scripts and the fastest way to see how the models compare on your own data.

Each compares FUTON against five representative baselines of the task at equal size: RFF, SIREN, FINER, Instant-NGP and TensoRF.

Notebook Signal Models Runtime on an A100 image_representation.ipynb data/Kodak/kodim19.png 6, about 197k parameters each, 1000 steps on the whole image about 6 minutes occupancy_volume.ipynb data/occupancy/lucy.ply at 512 voxels per unit length 6, about 131k parameters each, 1000 steps of \(2^{20}\) voxels about 7 minutes nerf.ipynb data/nerf/blender/lego under FINER's protocol, in a quick pass 6, about 75k parameters each, 5000 steps about 9 minutes (set NUM_STEPS = 25_000 for the benchmark's full schedule, about 25 minutes)

docs.title: Run them
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/pashtari/inro.git
cd inro
pip install -e ".[3d,nerf]" jupyterlab
python scripts/download_kodak.py --images 19
python scripts/download_meshes.py --meshes lucy
python scripts/download_blender.py --scenes lego
jupyter lab notebooks/

The notebooks read data from ../data/, relative to their folder, and are committed with their outputs, so they read without being run; rerun them top to bottom. The NeRF notebook also renders an orbit of its best INR as a GIF with imageio, which the nerf extra provides.

docs.title: What is inside
docs.text:
Each notebook is self-contained and has the same sections:

Section Content Setup Imports the packages, sets the seaborn theme and each model's color and marker, and defines the plotting helpers Data Shows the signal and the region the comparison magnifies Models Every model's constructor arguments and learning rate, with # deviation comments where a setting departs from the authors' code Training Runs inro.train or inro.nerf.train Convergence Plots the metric against steps and against training time Summary Tabulates every model's size, costs and scores, the best of each column in bold and the second underlined, and plots the scores against the costs Qualitative Comparison Sets the reconstructions side by side, magnified, above their errors

FUTON is drawn in black, and the baselines in seaborn's colorblind palette. The model settings are those of configs/<task>.yaml, which holds every model of the benchmark, the notebooks' and the rest.

docs.title: Occupancy volumes
docs.text:
A shape is represented as an occupancy INR \([-1, 1]^3 \to \{-1, 1\}\), fitted to a voxelized mesh and scored by intersection over union. This follows configs/occupancy.yaml and scripts/train_occupancy.py.

Lucy at about 131k parameters: every featured model's reconstruction with its IoU over the whole volume, and two regions magnified beneath it.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
OccupancyCoordinateDataset loads a mesh (any format trimesh reads, with the 3d extra) or an .xyz point cloud with normals, and then:

  1. Normalizesinto [−0.45, 0.45]³, as BACON and FINER do
  2. Markseach voxel center, resolution per unit length, inside or outside the shape
  3. Cropsto the occupied bounds, as WIRE does
  4. Cachesbeside the source, as .cache/<name>_<resolution>_centers.pt
import torch
import inro

path = "data/occupancy/lucy.ply"
train_set = inro.OccupancyCoordinateDataset(path, resolution=512, max_samples=2**20)
eval_set = inro.OccupancyCoordinateDataset(path, resolution=512)

eval_set.input.shape, eval_set.target.shape  # (depth, H, W, 3) coordinates, (depth, H, W, 1) targets in {-1, 1}
eval_set.original.shape                      # (1, depth, H, W) float occupancy in {0, 1}

A mesh's centers are tested with rays, a center being inside when most of five rays from it cross the surface an odd number of times, which tolerates the small holes of scanned meshes; a point cloud's take the sign of BACON's signed distance. Only centers decide, so a voxel that the surface merely crosses stays empty and thin parts keep their thickness. At 512 voxels per unit length a cropped volume holds 17 to 62 million voxels; max_samples=2**20 trains on 1,048,576 of them at random per step, as many for every shape. The five meshes of the benchmark are the Stanford armadillo, dragon, happy buddha, lucy and thai statue, fetched by scripts/download_meshes.py.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
The benchmark FUTON uses half the voxels along each axis of the cropped grid, a linear head, and the largest CP rank, a multiple of 5, that keeps it smaller than every baseline, the smallest of which has 131,585 parameters. Rank \(R\) costs \(R\) times the components plus one, and the head's bias adds 1, so Lucy's \(268 \times 154 \times 461\) grid gets 295, for 130,391 parameters:

components = [size // 2 for size in eval_set.grid_size]
rank = (131_584 - 1) // (sum(components) + 1) // 5 * 5
model = inro.FUTON(
    3, 1,
    basis=("cosine", {"num_components": components, "grid_size": eval_set.grid_size}),
    combiner=("cp", {"rank": rank}),
    head="linear",
    output_activation=torch.tanh,
)

On the voxel grid, which grid_size declares and which the crop sizes differently for every shape, the basis is evaluated once, when it is built, and each point reads its rows. The linear head contracts the whole grid at once when it has at most 64 cells per voxel of the batch, and otherwise combines each voxel's features from its rows. With \(2^{20}\) voxels per step, every benchmark shape takes the whole grid, and so does every full evaluation pass: Lucy's 19 million cells are 18 per voxel, the armadillo's 62 million 59.

docs.title: Training and evaluation
docs.text:
result = inro.train(
    model,
    train_set,
    eval_set,
    num_steps=1000,
    lr=3e-2,
    metrics={"iou": inro.iou},
    chunk_size=2**20,  # (1)!
    log_interval=50,
    eval_interval=50,
    save_reconstruction=False,
    log_dir="logs/tutorial/lucy/FUTON",
)
print(result["history"][-1]["eval"]["iou"])  # (2)!
  1. Voxels per evaluation pass, as many as per step: it bounds the memory of evaluating the whole volume.
  2. inro.iou thresholds the model's output at zero and compares it with the {0, 1} original.

Every model's IoU after the 1000 steps, and FUTON's convergence, are on the benchmarks page.

docs.title: Exporting a mesh
docs.text:
With the 3d extra, eval_set.save(volume, path) smooths the occupancy, runs marching cubes, writes a .dae mesh and renders it offscreen to a .png with Open3D, drawing the grid's axis up upwards: Lucy stands along the last, the other four shapes along the second, the default.

volume = inro.chunked_inference(model, eval_set.input, chunk_size=2**20)
occupancy = eval_set.postprocess(volume.cpu())  # (1, depth, H, W) in {0, 1}
eval_set.save(occupancy, "lucy_futon", up=2)    # lucy_futon.dae and .png

Rendering needs EGL and a GPU driver

Not every machine has them, which is why the call above and the benchmark script pass save_reconstruction=False and rebuild meshes from checkpoint.pt afterwards, with inro.evaluate(model, eval_set, ckpt_path=..., log_dir=...) on a workstation.

docs.title: The benchmark script
docs.text:
python scripts/train_occupancy.py                                       # all shapes, all models
python scripts/train_occupancy.py --data data/occupancy/lucy.ply --models FUTON

FUTON's ablations run on images; the ablations page reports them.
